en: *The Xuan-yi Shun-zheng-ji (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra), Volume One (with Preface)* Someone asked:
"Since ancient times, many have composed commentaries on the *Xuan-yi* of this sūtra.
Yet, the masters of Qiantang all maintain that the section on 'Contemplating the Mind' was arbitrarily added by later generations; only the Dharma Master Zhili of Siming has rescued it."

[He] thought: "My ancestors and relatives have personally taught this to others, and to this day there are none who do not transmit and practice it. For what reason do you now again alter and change it?

I fear that the multitude will not accept it and will be rejected by those in authority. In response, [I] say: What has ever been discarded in the current record regarding the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*)?
My concern is merely that Siming’s division of sections and his explanations of the meanings contain some errors and oversights, and furthermore...

To definitively establish that the three characters "Jin-guang-ming" (Golden Light) constitute a name based on a single dharma is not only inconsistent with the capacities of those who are sharp or dull, but also contradicts the doctrine of "preserving both.
Confucius said, "One must surely rectify names; if names are not correct, then speech will not be orderly.

Now, wishing to bring order to our speech by rectifying the names in order to uphold the words of the Patriarch and elucidate the intent of the Sūtra—is this not the work of one with "green eyes"? (i.e., a person of profound insight).
Was it abandoned and left unused? This preface was composed by the Śramaṇa of Yongjia, Shi Congyi, in the first month of the late spring on the Shangsi day of the year Jiazi,
the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era of the Imperial Song dynasty,
at the Vihāra of Baoji Teachings in Angu.
Part One: A General Overview, Divided into Two Sections. First, the title of the work explained:
*The Profound Meaning (Xuanyi) of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.

Regarding the term "Profound Meaning" (*xuanyi*), the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Fahua Xuanyi*) states that it is called "profound" (*xuan*) because it explains the sūtra through five meanings and comprehensively encompasses the five flavors (*wumi*).
Now, this should be stated as: "The title of the entire section is subsumed under the term 'Mysterious' (xuán). The *Wenju ji* states:

"Briefly citing the title of the scripture, it is said that the 'Mysterious' subsumes the entire section"—this is precisely what is meant. Furthermore, the *Dongjing fu* in the *Wenxuan* says: "Profound wisdom and mysterious insight," with the commentary stating: "Profound" refers to sagehood; "wisdom" refers to intelligence;
"mysterious" refers to pervasive penetration. The present case follows this same principle: "Mysterious" means pervasive penetration, which is to say, comprehensive subsumption (*tǒng*).
Furthermore, in the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), it quotes the *Guangya*: "The term 'mysterious' (*xuan*) refers to black; it signifies the profound stillness.
The *Yupian* states: "It means wondrous. The *Fahua Wenju* says: "Observing from afar and viewing mysteriously. The *Wenju Ji* explains:

"Because it is not restricted to a single direction, it is called 'viewing mysteriously'; being non-restrictive implies universality. This can be used as proof that the term "mysterious" (*xuan*) is universal. Moreover—

It is said that "examining the profound principle" constitutes "profound observation. Since the profound principle is itself the wondrous, this can be taken as proof that the "mysterious" (*xuan*) is the "wondrous" (*miao*).
Regarding the meaning [of these terms], the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states: "It is the reason for the name. Next is the teacher who expounds [the teaching].
The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai said that "Tiantai" is the name of the mountain where he resided, while "Zhizhe" (Wise One) was the title bestowed upon him by the Emperor of the Sui dynasty;

"Da" (Great) signifies his possession of great virtuous conduct, and "Shi" (Master) refers to him as a model for humanity. "Shuo" (to speak) means to delight; since the trigram Dui represents the mouth and tongue, it is used here to denote speech.
He provided sustenance for joy and delight, employing unimpeded eloquence with inexhaustible skill in exposition;

this was far different from other masters who grasp their pens to compose, only to revise and edit until they labor like one drawing silk from a cocoon. Next, the separate text is divided into two parts: first, the introduction; second, the formal explanation. The first part is further divided into two:
first, clarifying that the fundamental principle is beyond both speech and silence; second, clarifying the teaching that accords with conditions.

The first section of the text is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the essence of the Dharma, both in its horizontal and vertical dimensions and its depth and breadth; this is further divided into two sub-sections.
First, it presents the title and extols its virtues: the upper phrase presents the name of the scripture’s title, while the lower phrase extols the virtues of that title.
This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is profound and immeasurable.
The term "this" (*cīd*) is a word used for specific designation; according to the subsequent attached text, it is established as a name based on a particular phenomenon.
Therefore, the sutra text says, "this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*," and further states, "this is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*."
The title also refers to the matter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. Regarding the first three characters,孤山 (Gushan) calls them a "single metaphor," while 四明 (Siming) calls them a "single dharma.

Furthermore, in his commentary on the scriptural text, he explains that "this is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*" by using these characters to point directly to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), further demonstrating why it says:
"The Buddha wanders through immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, and therein abides."
When entering meditative concentration, he immediately proclaims, "This is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*," rather than saying, "The *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is like the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.

Therefore, the title is a designation for the phenomenon itself (*dharma*) alone; it does not derive from a metaphor. (And so forth. Now, I maintain that the principle established by Siming is incorrect.
Why? Because when the Buddha dwells within the *dharmatā*, he immediately proclaims, "This is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*," yet that which he dwells in...
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the Dharma-golden-light; this is like using a metaphor for a person of dull faculties.
For a person of sharp faculties, the phenomenon itself constitutes the metaphor. How can it be definitively stated that "this is the phenomenon" and "that is not the metaphor"?

Therefore, one knows that these characters in the sutra cannot directly point to the nature of phenomena in which one dwells. If, however, one were to directly point to the nature of phenomena in which one dwells...
The nature [of this sutra] not only does not conform to the title of the primary heading, but moreover runs counter to the capacities of those with sharp or dull faculties.

Therefore, one should know that since this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is both a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) and is itself composed of the entirety of the Dharma, its name is cited while its virtues are extolled;
hence it is called "this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, profound and immeasurable."
The commentary on the text states: "Because its essence encompasses the Dharma-realm, it is called 'immeasurable'; because it penetrates to the three truths, it is called 'profound.

It is not something that can be attained by those of the Two Vehicles or by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages. "Next, 'the great void space' and so forth further clarifies that worldly metaphors cannot exhaust [its nature]."
Even the great realm of empty space cannot serve as a metaphor for its height and breadth; how much less could the weight of Mount Meru or drops from the ocean ever reach its limits?
In the sutra, the four Buddhas offer four metaphors: first, that all waters might be known in their number of drops; second, ... [text continues] ... 2.
First, the weight of all Mount Sumerus could be known; second, the number of atoms in the great earth could be counted;

third, the boundaries of empty space could be discerned. Yet, among these four metaphors, even that which is all-pervasive—empty space—cannot serve as a metaphor for its [the Buddha's] height and vastness;
how much less, then, could the weights of mountains or the drops of the ocean ever be exhausted?
The "precipice" (*yá*) and the "steep height" (*xí gāo*) metaphorize the profound; the "breadth" (*guǎng*) and the "edge" (*biān*) metaphorize the immeasurable.

"Precipice" (*yá*)—the phonetic component is *jiā* (五佳切)—refers to a high cliff. "Níng" (寧), as explained in the *Fǔxíng* (輔行), is a term of aspiration (*yuàncí*), and it also means "how could it be" (*qǐ*).
One should know that the four Buddhas used as metaphors in the sutra represent the finite to illustrate the infinite; even the objects of measurement themselves are beyond thought.
The immeasurable dharmas known through calculation can never be fathomed; since they are immeasurable, they are likewise profoundly deep.
Thus, even the analogies of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*—such as the profound, immeasurable, and space-like—fall short of describing them.
Following the section on the sun’s orb, the next passage clarifies that the Supreme Sage can traverse what lower ranks cannot reach. This text consists of two parts: first, the analogy.
The blazing brilliance of the solar orb is not something an infant can gaze upon; how could a great ship with its multi-storied towers be held by one newly born?
It is because the substance of the sun is perfectly round that it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*); "blazing brilliance" refers to the height of its luminosity. An infant—
The *Cangjie pian* states: "A girl is called *ying*, and a boy is called *er*. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "It is a neck ornament (*jing-shi*). The *Shiming* states:

"That which is called an 'infant' (*ying-er*) at the beginning of human life is so named because the area before the chest is called the 'infant' (*ying*); thus, one holds the child before this 'infant' [spot] to suckle and nourish them.
The *Miaoxuan* quotes the *Dapin* (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), saying: "Great beings receive its radiance and employ the infant."
"Having lost its bright clarity": The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Shiqian) states that bodhisattvas and great beings receive the light of *prajñā*, whereby they possess the function regarding all phenomena;
since those of the two vehicles lack this function, it is compared to a seven-day-old infant who, upon looking at the solar disc, causes their eyes to lose their light—and thus it is called "losing.
This is because the illumination of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is not present within the light of *prajñā*.
This is because the clarity [of the meaning] lies entirely in its being like a state of mourning. *Bó* (pronounced with the *bǎng* and *bǎi* initials) refers to a large ship on the sea.
A *lóu* is a multi-storied building. A *lǔ* is a watchtower for defense atop a city wall; the *Shì míng* says: "A *lǔ* is 'exposed' (*lù*), as there is no roof covering it above.
The *Shuōwén* says it is a large shield. *Chǎn* means "to give birth. This metaphorical text appears in the... [source].
The verse from the *New Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* translated by Paramārtha states: "It is impossible for a newly born woman to hold up a great ship at sea laden with all manner of treasures.
One should know that in this passage, the blazing brilliance of the sun's orb is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom, which reaches the highest and is profoundly deep;
the great ship with its masts and galleries is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom, which is utterly vast.
"Immeasurable" refers to the infant, which is a metaphor for the *śrāvaka*; "newly born" is a metaphor for the *pratyekabuddha*. These are explained according to their specific distinctions.
If taken in a general sense, both the infant and the newly born serve as metaphors for both *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

If one were to use the infant specifically to metaphorize the *bodhisattva*, first, it would be an excessive deprecation; second, it would contradict the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Therefore, we know that [the infant] refers only to...
This is illustrated by the analogy of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas): even the sphere of action of the Buddha surpasses that which is practiced by the great bodhisattvas;
how much less could it be conceived by the minds of those of the two vehicles?

Therefore, the analogy states that the blazing orb of the sun is not something an infant can gaze upon, nor is it something that can be described by the words of those of the two vehicles. Thus, it is again illustrated as "Great."
The ships, towers, and battlements are not held by those who have newly arisen;

please observe the combined text, for its meaning will become manifest of itself, and there is no need to resolve it through some separate or divergent path. ○ From "All Buddhas" downwards, the next section combines the text into two parts: first, the formal combination.
Regarding "the sphere of activity of all Buddhas," the text states: "The sphere of activity of all Buddhas" precisely reveals that the Buddha-wisdom is immeasurable and profoundly deep;

because the Buddha-wisdom is immeasurable and profoundly deep, the sphere of activity is likewise immeasurable and profoundly deep; and because the sphere of activity is immeasurable and profoundly deep, [it reveals] the Buddha.
Wisdom is likewise immeasurable and profoundly deep; "lifting the box to reveal the lid" and "lifting the lid to reveal the box" refers precisely to this.
"Transcending the pure conduct of all bodhisattvas" is the definitive distinction.
It surpasses the pure conduct of all bodhisattvas, let alone the minds and speech of those of the two vehicles, which can hardly be conceived or described.
Because bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages below have not yet reached this ground, their wisdom and practice are unable to be so profound and vast.

When a bodhisattva abiding in the *Dharaṇī* stage attains the nine kinds of dhyāna, the first is called "essential nature" (*svabhāva*); upon entering this dhyāna, one immediately enters the purity of the *dharmatā*.
In this realm, even the followers of the Two Vehicles do not hear its name, let alone practice it.
If one enters the ninth stage of pure, purified dhyāna, both the general and specific afflictions and karmic burdens are exhausted, as well as the residual habits; therefore, it is called "pure.

The Buddha abides in this dhyāna, surpassing all bodhisattvas—how much more so than the followers of the Two Vehicles? Thus it is said: "How could the minds and mouths of the Two Vehicles [possibly reach it]?"
This is a reflection on the teaching. ○ Regarding the subsequent passage that rebukes ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), it is divided into two parts:
first, the direct rebuke. Ordinary people merely desire to speak, yet their speech harms the reality; they merely desire not to speak, yet their silence leads to error.
Neither is acceptable: if one wishes to speak, even speaking is not possible; if one wishes to remain silent, even silence is not possible.

"Ordinary" (*fan*) refers to those of common, worldly station who have not yet seen the Way. "In vain" (*tu*) means emptiness. "To speak" (*yan zhi*) means to produce verbal expressions, whether single, compound, or complete.
"To wound" (*shang*) means to damage. "Reality" (*shi*) refers to the principle of nature (*xingli*), which is without falsehood.
"Provisional" (*jia*) refers to that which is not spoken; regarding the four categories of singular, plural, complete, and so forth, each has one aspect that is "not spoken," which is simply silence.
As for "to lead to" (*zhi*), the *Yùpiān* states it means "to arrive at. "To lose" (*shī*) means to err or to deviate;

it necessarily leads to loss, and leading to loss necessarily results in injury to the reality. These are merely ornamental expressions appearing alternately; both are untenable when contrasted with what is spoken.

To remain silent is equally inappropriate; even if one were to cite scriptures and treatises to provide evidence for silence, this would merely reinforce attachment and increase views, which is not beneficial.
Since it is impossible to use speech to reach ultimate silence, both [speech and silence] are shown to be untenable.
Furthermore, those who have not yet attained realization give rise to four types of views regarding each of the four teachings and four gates.
Outside each of the four gates, there is likewise the "view of silence," which also harms reality and leads to error.

Thus, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), not a single dharma can be apprehended; yet ordinary people, upon encountering it, immediately engage in speech or silence and thereby grasp at it with attachment.
This is why they harm its true reality and incur these faults. Therefore, following the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the next section cites scriptural evidence.
The text is divided into two parts; first, it cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Thus, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, a brahmin says: "One does not attain this bodhi by means of internal contemplation, nor does one attain it by means of external contemplation, nor does one attain it by means of both internal and external contemplation."
Regarding the term "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*), the *Wenju ji* (Record of Words and Phrases) states: those who serve Brahmā while remaining at home are called Brahmins;

those who have left the household life among the non-Buddhist outsiders are generally called Nirgranthas. As for "not [seeing] within internal form," this means that wisdom is not seen within internal form;

the same applies to the four aggregates. "Not [seeing] within external form" means that wisdom is not seen within external form; the same applies to the four aggregates. "Neither internally nor externally" refers likewise.

However, "internal" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) and "external" refers to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Furthermore, one's own five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are called internal, while the five aggregates of others are called external.
Because the faculties and objects—whether belonging to oneself or others—are combined, they are called both internal and external.

According to the third phrase of the sutra, "neither internal nor external," this means it is not exclusively internal and not solely external; rather, it is the union of the internal and external. This precisely corresponds to the two [aspects].
This is also a phrase. The fourth phrase of that sutra says: "Nor is this wisdom attained by means of non-wisdom contemplation.
This is a phrase of dual negation. Since *bodhi* is the virtue of wisdom, there is no contradiction.
One should know that if there are views of internal or external and so forth, there is dwelling and attachment; if there is dwelling and attachment, it is not the sphere of activity of the Buddhas.

Because it is a place [beyond] such [grasping], the *Zhi guan* says: "If even a slight degree of faith cannot be found in the Brahmin Śreṇika while he still harbors attachment, how much less could there be the abandoning of the heterodox to enter the orthodox?
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:

"If there were even the slightest dharma to be apprehended within the Buddha-dharma, Śreṇika would never have given rise to faith in any dharma; how then could faith arise? Faith... [is thus established].
The Prajñāpāramitā does not abide by means of marks, nor by means of the absence of marks, because it does not grasp at marks;
thus it abides within the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita*). Question: Why is the case of Śreṇika cited here? Answer:

This sutra explains the emptiness of dharmas through various causes and conditions, to the point that not even the slightest mark can be apprehended. Consequently, people’s minds become suspicious and astonished, and they do not believe in this principle.
Because it is difficult to perceive, Subhūti says: if even within the Hīnayāna there is still the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), how much more so in the Mahāyāna?
Regarding the intent of this citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
first, as for Śreṇika, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there was a non-Buddhist brahmin named Dīrghanakha, also known as...
Śreṇika (and so forth). ○ Regarding the phrase "the Sūtra says next," this introduces the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says, "All are inconceivable and ineffable.
Although the scriptural text says "all are ineffable," following the same principle, it should be stated as "all are [inconceivable and] ineffable."
Because they are inconceivable, they are now said to be all "inconceivable teachings.
This is because conceptualizing the internal and external as equal, or explaining self and other as equal, both injure the reality and lead to error; therefore, both are inadmissible.

Furthermore, from "Moreover, regarding the arising of arising" onwards, the text clarifies the establishment of the teachings that accord with conditions (*pratyaya*). This section is divided into two parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent.
Furthermore, the arising of arising cannot be described; the non-arising of arising cannot be described; the arising of non-arising cannot be described;
and the non-arising of non-arising cannot be described. However, because there are causes and conditions, they can nevertheless be described.
The four phrases beginning with "the arising of arising is ineffable" conclude the preceding logical structure; according to the original teaching, both speech and silence are transcended.
However, because there are causes and conditions, it can also be said that "there are two phrases which give rise to subsequent teachings in accordance with conditions.

Regarding "the arising of arising," the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Because the Great Arising gives rise to the Small Arising, it is called 'the arising of arising. Furthermore, because of..."

Because it conditions the production of the produced dharmas, it is called "birth-production" (*jāti-jāti*); furthermore, because it gives rise to the birth of the fruit through the cause of birth, it is called "birth-production.
Even if one were to give rise to the fault of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) regarding this middle way, that too would belong to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), let alone other errors.
If one gives rise to the four attachments, there is not even the initial contemplation; therefore, it belongs to birth-and-death and is termed "birth-production. Thus:
The Tripiṭaka Teaching breaks through these types of arising and enters into nirvāṇa; this is called "non-arising.

This non-arising is named in dependence upon arising, thus it is called "arising-non-arising"—this is the Shared Teaching. In dependence upon the non-arising of the True, one speaks of the arising of the conventional;
this is called "non-arising-arising"—this is the Distinct Teaching. In dependence upon the extremes, one speaks of the Middle, wherein both extremes are broken as they arise.
These two—arising and non-arising—are non-arising, which is precisely the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Since the principle is not subject to the distinctions between the partial and the perfect among the four teachings, even "arising from arising" and so forth are all ineffable; if they cannot even be spoken of as the Perfect Teaching, how could they be spoken of according to the partial teachings?
Since speaking is impossible, silence is also impossible; both silence and speech are extinguished, for this very reason.
Regarding the statement that "because there are causes and conditions here, it can also be said," the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Notes) says:

In all textual passages, when something "cannot be said" is followed by what "can be said," this is because one must first realize it for oneself before necessarily transforming others. It further states:

Whether saint or ordinary person, anyone who wishes to benefit others must employ the fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to break through attachments both horizontally and vertically; only then can the four propositions be applied.
Compassion for others is the theme here; the present sutra precisely clarifies the principle of the ultimate fruit realized within oneself, which is ultimately ineffable.

Because there are causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it may also be explained in terms of "producing production" and so forth; this is merely the provisional use of names and marks within that which is nameless and markless.
Regarding these causes and conditions, both the *Miaoxuan* and the *Zhi guan* state that they refer to the ten types of dependent origination, beginning from ignorance (*avidyā*) and ending with...
Because it reaches the *bhavāṅgas* (factors of existence), it is said to be "ten. This has three meanings: first, establishing sentient beings; second, establishing the faculties and capacities;

third, establishing the vocal teaching. Regarding the establishment of sentient beings: based on two causes in the past and five fruits in the present, which mutually serve as causes and conditions, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are provisionally designated as "sentient beings.
Regarding the establishment of the faculties and capacities: in the past, one may have practiced either analytical [cessation]...
The substance consists of the distinct and perfect four practices; their function is to be moistened by ignorance, leading now to the five fruits.

Within these fruits of the aggregates (*skandha*), one further gives rise to either fundamental habitual tendencies or to the distinct and perfect [afflictions] of craving, grasping, and becoming. Those who establish the teaching of sound (*śabda-dharma*) give rise to craving, grasping, and becoming through analysis;
thus they evoke the Tripiṭaka Teaching. This is called "birth-giving birth," which cannot be fully described in terms of ten causes.
It can also be said that conditioned phenomena (*dharmas*) serve as the cause for the arising of "arising" (*jāti-jāti*);

the essence of this, as well as the distinctions between the various modes of arising and non-arising, and so forth—namely, the ten types of causal conditions (*pratyaya-dharma*)—should be understood according to this principle. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:

"Among the twelve links of dependent origination, 'birth and death' (*saṃsāra*) is not mentioned because it belongs to the future; here, we clarify the process from the past to the present to establish the conditions for the spiritual capacity (*nimita*)."
Therefore, it is not grasped. Thus, in the Great Sūtra, immediately following the passage on the "inexpressible," it states:
"The ten factors of dependent origination act as the cause for birth. Regarding what is meant by the ten factors of dependent origination acting as the cause for birth:

because seeds from previous lives within ignorance and volitional formations have come down to this present life, they again give rise to craving, grasping, and becoming based upon those original habitual tendencies.

Furthermore, based on hearing the Dharma in the present, one gives rise to the causes and conditions for practicing it herein. To speak briefly regarding the ten causes and conditions for sentient beings, the meaning should also encompass the causes and conditions of "response" (ganying).
That is to say, "response" refers to responding to the four types of Buddha-teachings, which is precisely the meaning of "causes and conditions" (yīnyuán) [and so forth].
Since this sutra belongs to the Vaipulya (fangděng) class, it universally encompasses the four categories beginning with "birth" (shēng). Therefore, the *Wénjù* explains it in this manner.
The preceding passages all refer to the four teachings (and so forth). ○ Regarding "Using gold as the name," the following section correctly clarifies the establishment of the doctrine;

that is, explaining the five chapters from the perspective of dependent origination. The text is divided into two parts: first, a general clarification that the established doctrine does not exceed the five major points of great meaning;
this is further divided into two, the first of which is the actual presentation of the five chapters.
It is named "Gold" because its name surpasses all other jewels; it takes the *dharmatā* as its essence, meaning that it is the adorned realm wherein the Tathāgata dwells;
it takes the profound and wondrous merits of the bodhisattvas as its primary principle; and it takes the illumination of the various heavens and the generation of joy in their hearts as its function.
Therefore, in text it is titled the "King of Sutras," and in its teaching it encompasses all scriptures.
"Gold is used as the name" means that it is employed for its function. When the Buddha spoke this sutra, he used "Golden Light" (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*) as its specific title;
although the word "gold" alone is indicated in the text, one must necessarily discuss the light in relation to gold. This is because [gold] is the foremost among all jewels.

The character *gài* (蓋) is a particle used to assist the syntax, and it also serves as an introductory phrase. As for "all jewels": (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding "all jewels," but the translation reflects the complete syntactic unit available.)
Although jewels are numerous, they do not exceed seven kinds: first, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; fourth, crystal;
fifth, mother-of-pearl; sixth, red pearl; and seventh, agate (the names of these seven treasures vary across sūtras and śāstras; for now, these are cited).
Because gold is the foremost among the seven treasures and because all sūtras and śāstras list it at the beginning, it is said that the name is derived from gold.
Its name surpasses all other jewels. If one with dull faculties uses the analogy to represent the Dharma, they will compare this gold to the *dharmatā*;
if one with sharp faculties takes the Dharma as the analogy, then the gold is the *dharmatā*.
If it were not so, how could the name "gold"—which surpasses all other jewels—be explained?

This [objection] is therefore erroneous; this initial designation of the title is even more trustworthy, and those of clear discernment should examine it carefully without requiring further elaboration.

Nevertheless, fearing that later generations might be deluded by others, I must further distinguish it. Siming stated: "The three characters of the separate title refer to the Dharma itself and are not metaphors.
He further said: "It takes 'Jin-guang-ming' (Golden Light) as its name; it is because of the Golden Light..."

To claim that its substance (*tattva*) is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, its essence (*śāstra*) is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, and its application (*prayojana*) is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as its doctrinal characteristic (*śāstralakṣaṇa*)—this we say is not so.
Why? Because this text clearly demonstrates that it takes "Gold" (*suvarṇa*) as its name and "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) as its substance;
furthermore, by its title as the "King of Sūtras," it subsumes all other scriptures. How could it ever be treated as a single uniform entity based solely on the term "Suvarṇaprabhāsottama"?
Is it the essence, the doctrine, the function, or the characteristics of the teaching?

If you claim that the specific title refers to the Dharma (the reality) rather than the metaphor, then the text here ought to be revised to read "taking *dharmatā* as the name. If that were the case, how could the Tathāgata’s way of wandering through the world be so utterly inverted?
Question: If this is so, why does [the text] not say "taking the metaphor as the name," but instead specifically designate it thus?
To answer this question by using "Gold" as the title is excellent; it is well able to dispel the delusions of the multitude. Why is this?

If, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the four characters of its specific title mean "The Wondrous Dharma is a Lotus," then since the text clearly establishes this as a metaphor, it is said that the title consists of both the Dharma and the metaphor.
However, in the present sutra, although the scriptural text speaks of the "profound dharmatā," it is "gold."
In the separate title of the *Guangming* (Radiance), it merely says "Three-Character *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*" and does not mention the "immeasurable and profound *dharmatā*.

Therefore, it is specifically designated by the name "Gold" (*suvarṇa*) not only to show that the three characters of the separate title are subsumed under a single metaphor, but also to manifest that the sharp and dull faculties, as well as the near and distant [audiences], cannot be discarded. Why is this so? If...
Those of dull faculties understand the three characters of the distinct title through the analogy that illustrates the Dharma;

they realize that these three characters of the distinct title serve as an analogy for the infinitely profound *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) found within the sutra text. Conversely, those of sharp faculties take the Dharma itself as the analogy;
they realize that the infinitely profound *dharmatā* of the sutra text serves as the analogy for the three characters of the distinct title. It is simply this.

Using phenomena as metaphors is the interpretation of our own school; this is termed "distant," for it takes the Dharma itself to serve as a metaphor. Taking the Dharma as the primary subject is the true intent of this sutra;

this is termed "proximate. Although they differ in being distant or proximate, if one examines them through the lens of our school’s seven types of titles, these cases are neither a combination of multiple elements nor a single phenomenon, nor a single person. Why? If one were to say it is a single [element]...
Since the Dharma is identical to the sutra text and the profound *dharmatā*, why is it not titled the *Dharmatā Sūtra*?
Why must it be titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*? Furthermore, how does it differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and so forth?
Since it is neither a single dharma nor a single person, if one does not categorize it by means of a single metaphor within the "single threefold" [classification], then—like...
Regarding the question of which category this belongs to, some who have not seen [the full text] hear that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is a "single metaphor" (ekopama) and immediately raise the objection:

"How does this differ from the ancient masters? Alas! How lamentable it is that one's hands, once stuck in glue, are so difficult to release; that one is so hard to awaken from a dream—even to such an extent!

One should know that the present work establishes a distinct three-character title, using "Gold" (*suvarṇa*) as its name, which is subsumed under the category of the single metaphor while also extending its application to other aspects.
Using the analogy for dull faculties to represent the Dharma collects the third analogy mentioned below;
using the Dharma itself as the analogy for sharp faculties collects the fourth and fifth analogies mentioned below. How could it be a mistake to listen to the text as it stands?
To criticize the text based on its literal phrasing is the view of the ancient masters. Yet even those ancient masters were not exhaustive in their use of analogies to represent the Dharma.

How could the feet possibly understand the application of metaphors to the dharmas themselves? Since the subsequent text states that "metaphors are applied to the dharmas themselves," how can Sizong Ming say they are "single dharmas"?
Now I ask Sizong Ming: what does he point to as the dharma, and what does he point to as the metaphor?
How can a metaphor be applied to the dharma itself? Let him answer this, and his words will naturally contradict one another. For if he points to—
Regarding the phrase "the dharma-nature of the sūtra-text" (*sūtra-pada-dharmatā*), it is not yet clear what is being pointed to as the object of this analogy.

If one points to the sūtra-text itself—namely, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*—as the object of the analogy, then one must consider whether these three characters of the distinct title constitute the "dharma" or the "analogy.
If they are said to be the "dharma," then since the dharma-nature of the sūtra-text is already the "dharma," would the three characters of the distinct title also [be the dharma]?

Furthermore, if this dharma were to take the entirety of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) to become the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, it would constitute the metaphor of "the dharma itself becoming the dharma.

To observe this through such a perspective: the term "dharma-nature" within the scriptural text is designated as the "dharma," while the three characters of the distinct title are designated as the "metaphor.
Thus, if the entirety of the dharma-nature becomes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, it perfectly accords with the metaphor of "the dharma itself becoming the metaphor."
This teaching employs both direct correspondence and metaphorical analogy to illustrate the Dharma without contradiction. Why is this?

It uses the metaphor of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* to illustrate the Dharma-nature, and takes the entirety of the Dharma-nature to serve as the metaphor for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. The Buddha’s words are skillful and the meaning of the sutra is profound;
were it not for our Patriarch Zhiyi’s marvelous awakening and illumination, who else could have reached such a realization?
The reason for establishing this title is simply to state that it is "named after gold.

As for the third analogy in the subsequent text, the fourth which is appended to the passage, and the fifth which refers to the essence itself—when their meanings are merged, they take *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as their essence.
Regarding the meaning of "that in which the Tathāgata dwells," Zhiyi (Four Illuminations) states: "Meaning (*artha*) is precisely the ultimate *paramārtha* (supreme truth). Now...

This means it is not so. What is the meaning? "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the "reason" (*so-yi*). As for this "reason," it is because [the term] speaks of the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) as penetrating both cause and fruit.
Now, since the Buddha’s "wandering" takes *dharmatā* as its essence, this distinguishes it from the *dharmatā* contemplated during the causal stage;

therefore, it is called "meaning. Thus, how could the "meaning" in the phrase "that which the Tathāgata wanders in" be indiscriminately conflated with the term "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) to explain the current word "meaning"?

If one were to say that the cause is different from the fruit, then the cause would not truly be a cause; for it is understood that the fruit arises from the cause, and only through the cause does the fruit finally achieve its realization.
The *Four Heavenly Kings Chapter* states: "Adorning the profound and wondrous merits and virtues of a Bodhisattva. The commentary on this passage explains:

"In terms of the essence of practice, [this] enables the Bodhisattva to possess the two adornments and achieve the ultimate fruit. Since it speaks of "adornment," we know this is a praise of the fundamental tenet (*zong*).
It also illuminates the various heavens, causing the hearts of the devas to rejoice; as stated in the Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings:
"It is constantly revered by all the devas, able to cause the hearts of the heavenly kings to rejoice, and it is also praised by the World Protectors (*Lokapālas*).
This sutra can illuminate the palaces of the various devas; this sutra can bestow happiness upon sentient beings."

This sutra can cause the rivers of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals to burn up, dry out, and wither away, even to the point that—summarizing the essential meaning—it is said that this sutra can extinguish the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings.

The commentary on the text explains: "Worldly devas, Pure devas, and Dharma devas" (as taught in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, Chapter on the Virtuous King). [It lists] four kinds of devas: first, worldly devas, such as various kings; second, birth-devas...

The "Four Kings" and those above them constitute the first; the "Three Pure Heavens" refer to those from the first fruit (srotāpanna) upward; the "Dharma-Heaven" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes who perceive the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatārtha*). [Note: Only three are mentioned here, likely because the "Heaven of Rebirth" was omitted.
All these take the ultimate stage as their object of veneration and transcend the offerings of the three karmas.

Furthermore, from the hells below up to the Bodhisattvas, as long as ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted, there is universally the presence of feverish affliction (*paridāha*); this sutra can remove it, making one as cool and refreshing as the moon—know this!

The praise expressed in the subsequent passage—stating that "all realms of existence are completely parched" and "the three miserable paths are cleared of heat and affliction"—should be understood according to this principle.
Thus, the title "King of Sutras," which indicates that the teaching encompasses all scriptures, is established by the character "guo" (國/王) within the text itself.
Although the title "King of Sutras" applies generally to all chapters, it specifically refers here to the beginning of the "Four Heavenly Kings Chapter."

This is because the texts concerning the application of the school all rely upon the beginning of the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings. Thus, the *Sutra of Golden Light* states in the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings":
"This subtle and wondrous *Golden Light Sūtra* is the king of all sūtras, protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

The commentary on the words and phrases explains: "The principle of the dharma-nature is what the Buddhas protect and remember; since the text elucidates this principle, it is called a 'sūtra' (*sūtra*)."

Since the King [of Sutras] has already spoken, the King knows this to be the praise of its essence (*tattva*). Furthermore, the *Introduction Chapter* (*Nidāna-parivarta*) states, "The king of all sutras.

The commentary on these words explains it as describing the essence; yet now it is called a title of the text. As for the phrase "the teaching of the King of Sutras encompasses all scriptures," if this refers to that which is expressed (*vācya*), it belongs to the description of the essence;
if it refers to the expressive medium (*vācaka*), it constitutes the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).
Now, because it follows that which expresses [the meaning], it is called the "characteristic of the teaching" (*śāstralakṣaṇa*).

If it were not so, how could one interpret the textual designation "included within the teaching"? Therefore, one must know that the text itself is the teaching. Since the principle expressed is what the King [of Teachings] governs and encompasses, the expression must correspond to that which is expressed;
thus, the textual teaching encompasses all scriptures. Furthermore, the characteristic of the teaching is merely a differentiation of what preceded.

Regarding these four chapters, the first four penetrate both phenomena and principle; thus, they are titled "Kings of Sūtras" (*sūtrarāja*) as they encompass all scriptures through their relationship of means and end.
While there is no contradiction between the means and the end, we shall for now follow the perspective of the expressive medium and therefore categorize them under "Teaching" (*śāsana*).

As for "all scriptures," the doctrinal characteristics of this sūtra represent the third stage, the "Equal and Perfect" (*samatā-samyak*), which is like clarified butter (*ghṛta*); the meanings elucidated by the four teachings properly correspond to this stage of penetration.
The teaching immediately brings forth the distinct [teachings] while clarifying the perfect;

furthermore, because the Vermilion Bird Gate does not obstruct the common people, the Great likewise subsumes the Small—the reason for this statement regarding the various scriptures is precisely due to this.

Thus we know that since the texts of the various sections of the Hīnayāna are not titled "Kingly Sūtras," their teachings do not subsume the various scriptures. ○ Therefore, "only named next" concludes and indicates [the meaning].

Therefore, "precious" (*jin*) alone is its name, "gold" (*jīn*) alone is its essence, "profound" (*shēn*) alone is its tenet, "great" (*dà*) alone is its function, and "sovereign" (*wáng*) alone is its teaching.
Since "precious" is the name for that which is supreme among all jewels, one knows that "precious" alone is its name; because it is a precious gold...
It is because it is supremely and uniquely noble; "only" (*kevala*) means unique.

Since its essence is the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and this is where the Tathāgata dwells, it takes the ultimate as its essence, for this essence is precisely where the ultimate fruit dwells.

Since it takes the profound and wondrous merits of the Bodhisattva’s adornments as its primary principle (*śāstra*), it takes the profound alone as its principle; through these causes, the ultimate fruit is accomplished.
It is supreme because it is not shallow; it illuminates the minds of all the devas and causes them to give rise to joy, which serves as its function.
It is "Great" alone because its power to extinguish evil and produce good is vast and extensive.
Its title is called the "King of Sūtras" because its teaching encompasses all dharmas; thus, the teaching that expresses is named after the principle it expresses.

This also comprehensively encompasses [the teaching] without omission; the skeletal outline of the five major points of great meaning lies herein. To recognize the general purport of the present section, it shall be understood from the text below.
Next, the text clarifies that the essence of non-duality is constantly praised by all the sages.
This section is divided into two parts. First, the main explanation, which is further divided into five parts. First, the clarification of the protection and maintenance by all Buddhas.
Therefore, the essence of non-duality is constantly protected and sustained by the four World-Honored Buddhas; it is likewise so throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions.

What was previously stated—that the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is the essence—refers to the sphere in which the Tathāgata dwells; what is now stated as "the reason why it is non-dual" refers to this same principle.
Because the essence is constantly protected and sustained by the four Buddhas, we know that what is said here is identical in meaning to what was stated previously.
This refers to the fact that the nature-essence is not only the sphere where the Tathāgata dwells, but is also constantly protected and sustained by the four Buddhas;
the reason for using the term "so-yi" (the reason why) is precisely due to this. Therefore, the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states: "Śākyamuni’s awakening wisdom."

Sharing the same Dharma-nature as the four Buddhas, the four virtues are the meaning of the essence (*tattva*); the manifestation of the fruit-wisdom that reveals this essence is the meaning of the thesis (*siddhānta*);
and providing protection against perversions and severing doubt is the meaning of the function (*kāritra*).

Although the thesis is presented as primary, it does not obstruct the essence, for it takes up the Dharma-nature and its four virtues which are protected and sustained. Regarding the term "non-dual" (*advaya*), "duality" refers to height.
Because the principle of the dharma-nature is vast, profound, immeasurable, non-dual, and neither high nor vast, the dharma-nature simultaneously illuminates both [aspects]:
it is dual while being non-dual, and non-dual while being dual.

As for "protecting and maintaining," it means protecting so that delusions do not arise and maintaining so that the principle is not lost. Since the awakened wisdom of the four Śākyamuni Buddhas is already...
The same is true for the three periods of time and the ten directions; is it not the case that the Way of all Buddhas is identical? Therefore, the sutra below states:
"If you wish to know the sphere of practice of all Buddhas of the three periods, you should listen to and receive this wondrous sutra.
It further states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions constantly keep this sutra in mind. Since Śākyamuni and the four Buddhas are currently present, they are included as well.
The four cardinal directions serve as the model for the past and future; likewise, it is so for the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir.
Therefore, it is said that the three periods of time and the ten directions are also thus. ○ Next, the passage beginning with "All" clarifies the remote prostration of the Bodhisattvas.
"All Bodhisattvas from the various directions pay homage from afar.
The *Praise of the Buddha Chapter* states: "Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva assemblies depart from this world for the land of the Tathāgata Golden Jewel Canopy Mountain King;
having arrived in that land, they prostrate before the Buddha. The commentary on these words and phrases says:

The *Cenlie zan* (Praise of the Array) states that from this world-system to the *Suvarṇaratnacchatra* (Golden Jewel Canopy) world-system, the Bodhisattvas now pay homage throughout all other directions.
The reason why these Bodhisattvas universally pay remote homage to Śākyamuni in other directions is precisely because the introduction describes the general principle:
that the Tathāgata dwells within the profound and vast *dharmatā*, manifesting for the benefit of beings from beginning to end.
Since all these are the great essence, wisdom, and function of the Tathāgata, the bodhisattvas praise the Buddha and extol this teaching as well as its Teacher.
[Section on] the Tree Deity: the third part clarifies how the tree deity extols [the Buddha].
The tree goddess, a virtuous woman, personally shed tears as she praised him.
In the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha," the praise by the tree goddess says: "I constantly practice the supreme and great compassion, weeping and shedding tears in my desire to see the Buddha.
Excellent, Tathāgata! You have entered the sphere of action of all Buddhas, which is perfectly tranquil."
The Great City of Immaculate, Pure, and Profound Samādhi. [Section on] All the Heavens Beneath the Four Illuminations: All the heavens cover and benefit [the practitioner].
This is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation;
second, the specific manifestations. The various heavens cover him with celestial majesty, the earth deities nourish him with terrestrial fertility, and eloquence is added to his eloquence.
The Way benefits through its merits, while wealth and treasures augment it.

As for the phrase "the various devas cover it with celestial majesty," the *Caturmahārājakāyika-parivarta* states that this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is constantly protected and sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the devas; "covering" here means protection. The terrestrial deities moisten it.
Regarding the term "earth-fertility" (*dìfēi*), "earth-deity" (*dìqí*) refers to the earth-spirit (*dìshén*).
Heavenly deities are called *líng* (spirits), earth deities are called *qí* (deities), and human deities are called *guǐ* (ghosts). The section on Earth Deities states:

"In whatever place this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* is disseminated, I shall always act as its guardian therein; beneath the Dharma-seat, I shall bear its feet upon my head. Thus have I heard.

The Dharma has already increased the strength of my body, and this great earth has acquired all manner of flavors; its growth is complete, and its rich, fertile soil is more abundant and succulent than it was today.
As for the Great Eloquence (Mahāpratibhāna) who adds eloquence to the Path, the *Mahāpratibhānadevaputra-parivarta* says:
"Regarding this speaker of the Dharma, I shall augment his joy in speaking and his eloquence," and so on, up to: "he is able to bring forth [all qualities]."
That which attains *sambodhi* at death is the Path; furthermore, eloquence and great wisdom are themselves the discernment of the Path.
Regarding the augmentation of merit through wealth and treasures, the "Chapter on the Goddess of Merit" states:

"If there is anyone who can recite this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and thereby make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, it should be known that such a person is able to accumulate [merit]."

Regarding the accumulation of wealth and treasures, it is further said that for the sake of the Dharma-preacher, I shall provide whatever is required—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other assets—so that there shall be no lack whatsoever.

One should know that this benefit to humanity, provided by celestial deities and terrestrial spirits, exists solely for the purpose of circulating the Dharma; it would not be so if the Dharma were not propagated.
The Dharma is merely for those who, out of greed, look up to the various sages; those who desire to seek further benefit may fear that their efforts will be in vain.

○ Regarding the passage "All those who," the following section simultaneously demonstrates both the essence and the function [of the teaching]. This text is divided into two parts: first, citing the text on the extinction of evil to clarify its function.
"All realms of existence are completely dried up; the three miserable paths are cleared of their feverish afflictions.
