Below, under the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), there follows a detailed explanation of the four virtues of the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body is eternal because it is free from the two kinds of death; it is blissful because it does not undergo the two extremes; it is self because it possesses the eight masteries;
and it is pure because its bodily, verbal, and mental actions are purified. To illustrate these four virtues of the Dharma-body through worldly analogies:
just as gold remains unchanging, unstained, and transforms into wealth and nobility, so too is the Dharma-body. Thus, the world’s gold serves as a metaphor for them.
The Dharma-body is eternal because it is free from the two types of death—the death of the physical body (*pariccheda*) and the death of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Since the Dharma-body does not undergo these two deaths, it is eternal. Because both extremes are suffering and the Dharma-body as the Middle Way is not subject to them, it is called bliss.
Furthermore, because the Dharma-body possesses the eight kinds of mastery, it is called self. And because its three karmas are pure, it is called pure.
Therefore, because the four virtues of the Dharma-body are without deficiency, it is called the "virtue of the Dharma-body.

As for the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*), the name appears in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtras* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, where they are termed the "eight miraculous transformations" (*aṣṭarddhi-prātihārya*).

Regarding "miraculous transformation," it refers to that which suddenly exists where there was nothing, and suddenly ceases to exist where it once was. Regarding "mastery," it means that all things are operated upon without deliberation and without obstruction. Thus it is said.
The substance is the same as that in the *Mahā-śāstra*, though the terminology differs slightly; I shall now set them forth in full. The eight supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) are:
first, the ability to become small; second, the ability to become large; third, the ability to become light; fourth, the ability to attain mastery; fifth, the ability to possess sovereignty;

sixth, the ability to travel to distant places; seventh, the ability to shake the earth; eighth, the ability to act according to one’s will. The eight masteries (*vaśitā*) are: first, the ability to manifest as one...
1. To manifest many bodies, as numerous as motes of dust; 2. to fill a great trichiliocosm with a single mote of dust-sized body; 3.
to lift a body the size of a great trichiliocosm and travel far away with ease; 4. to manifest in immeasurable forms while always dwelling in a single land;
5. to employ the faculties of all senses interchangeably; 6. to attain all dharmas while remaining free from the notion of dharmas; 7. to preach...
A single verse [is realized] after immeasurable kalpas; eighth, the body is like empty space, appearing and disappearing as appropriate.
The Dharma-body of the Middle Way is inherently possessed; when these eight qualities are present, it is only then called "virtue. "Type" (lei) means comparison; "forceful" (qiang) means provisional;
"entrusted" (ji) means to rely upon; "worldly gold" (shi jin) is gold within the world; "analogy" (pi) refers to a metaphorical illustration.
Furthermore, "analogy" (*yù*) means to clarify through instruction; it involves relying on this to compare with that, or entrusting the shallow to instruct the profound.
It is like using the shaking of a tree to instruct on the wind, or raising a fan to illustrate the moon.

Thus, in the world, gold—whose color does not change and whose substance is unstained, transforming without obstruction and bringing about wealth and nobility—is used as a sequential analogy for the four virtues of the *dharmakāya*: permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Since the illustration of the Dharma is thus, one should understand that the Dharma serves as the illustration by reversing this.
○ Next, the four virtues of Prajñā are explained.

Prajñā spontaneously possesses these four virtues because wisdom is in silent accord with suchness, as it is with its object. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Because form is pure, Prajñā..."
If one applies this same principle to purity (*śuddhi*), then the meanings of "the permanence of form," "the bliss of form," and "the self of form" are all established.
Furthermore, it is said: "Because form is great, Prajñā is great; because form is boundless, Prajñā is boundless.
This is the vastness of *dharmatā*; likewise, Prajñā is also vast. Applying this analogy, one should say: "Because form is profound, Prajñā is also profound. This is *dharmatā*.
The height of wisdom (*prajñā*) is also the height of the suchness (*tathatā*).
When wisdom is darkly merged with suchness, as if it were the object itself, wisdom is precisely *prajñā* and the object is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Because wisdom and its object are united, they are said to be "darkly merged" (*ming*). Since the subject and object correspond to one another, both the object and wisdom are referred to as [suchness]. Therefore, the text from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is cited.
Since the *Prasādapratibhānaprātihārya-sūtra* already contains the pure virtues of *prajñā*, how could it possibly lack the three [attributes] of permanence, bliss, and self?
Therefore, it is said that by analogy with this, all meanings such as the permanence of form (*rūpa*) and so forth are established. For this reason, one should say:
"Because form is permanent, *prajñā* is permanent; ... up to ... because form is self, *prajñā* is self. It is also said: "Form is great (*mahat*)."
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) here cites the scriptural passage stating that because the *dharmatā-rūpa* (the form of the nature of phenomena) is vast, the *prajñā* (wisdom) is also vast;
this clarifies that because the *dharmatā* of this present sutra is vast and immeasurable, the *prajñā* is likewise vast and immeasurable.
"Boundless" (*ananta*) means extensive. By analogy with these [terms], one explains its height, depth, and profound mystery through this vastness and immeasurability.
This is also an example of explaining the vertical through the horizontal. Regarding the phrase "One should know," etc., this is the conclusion and demonstration.
One should know that it is clear that Prajñā also possesses the four virtues.
It is evident that Prajñā not only possesses these four virtues, but also possesses immeasurable and profound meanings, all of which are fully realized.
This is what is meant by that. ○ Third, the explanation of the four virtues of liberation.
Liberation also possesses the four virtues. Now, as for liberation: when all evils are forever exhausted, then impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity have all been exhausted.
Furthermore, it is the universal convergence of all virtues; that is, permanence, bliss, self, and purity are universally converged.

Furthermore, the four [truths] such as impermanence are the dharmas practiced by the Hīnayāna; if viewed from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, they are still termed "perversions" and thus belong to the various evils.
Since the absence of these four is called liberation, it is said that one is "liberated from all evils."
"Permanently exhausting" refers to the exhaustion of the four [marks], such as impermanence and so forth.

If liberation exhausts these four—impermanence and the rest—it must necessarily be in vast union with permanence, bliss, self, and purity; though there is a sequence in their explanation, in principle there is no difference in time. "Vast" (溥) means extensive;
"union" (會) means convergence. Next, citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* to clarify that true liberation is the Tathāgata, this explains liberation.

Liberation is endowed with the three virtues. Since the preceding passage, in its explanation of the [three bodies], clarified only that the *dharmakāya* possesses all dharmas and that through *prajñā* one awakens to and realizes the three truths, it now clarifies that liberation itself possesses these three.
First, it is shown that liberation is endowed with the *dharmakāya*; therefore, what is called "true liberation" is precisely the *tathatā* (suchness).
Come. ○ Next, the Mahāyāna Sūtra is cited.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "True liberation is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Dharmakāya. One should know that liberation is identical to the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "The complete possession of the three dots is called Great Nirvāṇa."
One should know that the three dots (*bindu*) are syllables; the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti are all syllables.
Therefore, one knows that these three dots fully possess the four virtues. Thus it is said that being endowed with the three causes is precisely the three wisdoms.

Each of the three wisdoms possesses the four virtues, and the fullness of the three virtues is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). One must know that the syllable of this "endowment" necessarily possesses the four virtues. This is how it should be understood.
The possession of the four virtues is its characteristic.
The possession of the three points is the complete perfection of liberation and the three virtues; furthermore, it is said that the three causes are the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Next, it clarifies that liberation also possesses the three wisdoms; since *prajñā* is wisdom, [it is established] by means of the three causes.
That is to say, these are the three wisdoms; thus, in the present text, liberation possesses the four virtues. It is not only endowed with the three virtues, but also endowed with the three wisdoms.
This serves as proof that the preceding text’s discussion of the Dharma-body and Prajñā should likewise be understood in this way;

it is merely a matter of the elegant phrasing of the preceding and succeeding sections mutually illustrating one another. Only in this manner can one see that the three dharmas possess nine dharmas, and that the nine dharmas are [the three dharmas].

These are the three dharmas. Regarding what is called the "Secret Treasury" (Guhyakośa), which is the perfection of the three points and three virtues, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Lamentation," says:
"What is meant by the 'Secret Treasury'? It is like the three dots of the letter *I*. If they are placed side-by-side, they do not form an *I*;
if they are placed vertically, they likewise do not form one. Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara does it become so."
The formation of the character "E" (伊) from three dots does not constitute "E" if they are separate; I understand it in this same way.
The dharma of liberation is not nirvāṇa, the body of the Tathāgata is not nirvāṇa, and Mahāprajñā is also not nirvāṇa.
If these three dharmas were distinct from one another, they would not be nirvāṇa. I now abide in these three dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
Therefore, one enters *nirvāṇa* like the worldly letter "I" (*ī*). Zhanran says that this explains the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*), and its text is divided into three parts:
first, a simile for the three dots; second, a simile for the three eyes; and third, the unification of these with the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*). From the passage "From now on I abide...

onwards, the fourth part is the conclusion regarding the Secret Treasury. "Abiding in the three dharmas" concludes the section on the Three Virtues, and "entering *nirvāṇa*" [concludes the preceding].

The "binding" (*bandhana*) refers to the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), which is like the worldly letter *i* formed by binding three dots. The text is abbreviated and does not explicitly show the binding of the "Heavenly Eye" (and so forth).

Although the current text cites the meaning of the three dots as the secret treasury, its significance must encompass the second [section] on the three eyes, the third on the three virtues, and the fourth on their formation.
Next, the passage beginning with "If one attains... explains the remaining nine dharmas. The text is as follows:
Second, first concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent:
"If one grasps the meaning of this one chapter, the remaining nine can be understood. Unable to remain silent, I shall speak further in brief.

Since one example illustrates all others, it is said they "can be understood"; yet for those who have not yet fully realized this, I shall speak further in brief. The word "already" (*yi*) serves to conclude.
Nor can it be brought to rest through silent stillness. ○ Next, regarding the section beginning with "How so," the remaining nine passages are correctly explained in nine parts;
first, the explanation of the Three Jewels is divided into three sections, the first of which is the direct explanation.
What are the three? What are the jewels? The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha constitute these three. That which is worthy of honor and respect is called a "jewel.

The principle that is worthy of honor is called the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*). The wisdom that awakens to this principle and is worthy of honor is called the Jewel of the Buddha (*buddharatna*).
Vairocana pervades all places; when phenomena are such that they are identical with the principle, this harmony that is worthy of honor is called the Jewel of the Sangha (*saṃgharatna*).
Vairocana is translated here as "pervading all places. However, in principle there is nothing that exists; it pervades all phenomena. Thus, within phenomena itself lies the principle.
This harmony is venerable and is named the Jewel of the Sangha. Following this, the subsequent section is integrated with what precedes it.
These Three Jewels are all eternal, blissful, self, and pure; because they are eternal, blissful, self, and pure, they are worthy of honor and reverence.
One should know that these three virtues and the Three Jewels are non-dual and without distinction.
Now, Yong [states]: "The Three Jewels (triratna) encompass the aforementioned three virtues; they are worthy of veneration precisely because they possess virtue.
Since that which possesses virtue is worthy of veneration, is it not indeed a 'jewel'? Therefore, one should know that the three virtues and the Three Jewels are non-dual and without distinction.
Regarding this 'non-duality and lack of distinction,' for example, the *Fahua wenju* says 'non-dual and non-different. The *Wenju ji* explains:"
Furthermore, by reiterating "non-different" one reinforces "non-duality"; it is precisely because there is no difference that it is called non-dual.
Now this case is likewise: by reiterating "no distinction" one reinforces "non-duality"; it is precisely because there is no distinction that it is called non-dual.
As for the term "non-dual," it means the essence is one; it is precisely because there is no distinction that the oneness is revealed. [Section] Three: Since... (text fragment)
The lower section follows the precedent of using analogies;
since the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (Golden Light) was used as a metaphor for the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), it is now likewise used as a metaphor for the Three Jewels (*triratna*).

The Three Jewels and the Three Virtues are non-dual and without distinction. Since the three characters of the distinct title were previously used as metaphors for the Three [Virtues], [the same applies here].
For this reason, following the established precedent, three characters are used to illustrate the Three Jewels;

since the analogy for the Dharma is thus constituted, the application of the Dharma as an illustration can be understood by reversing this. All subsequent passages should be interpreted according to this principle.
Next, the explanation of the three types of *nirvāṇa* consists of three parts: first, the formal explanation.
What are the three? What is the nature of nirvāṇa? They are: natural purity, perfect purity, and purity through skillful means;
these are the three. That which is neither arising nor ceasing is called nirvāṇa. The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena cannot be defiled and cannot be purified.

Non-defilement is non-arising; non-purification is non-ceasing. This is called "nirvāṇa of natural purity. By practicing the causes in accordance with the principle, delusion ultimately does not arise, and wisdom is perfected.
Ultimately, there is neither extinction nor arising; this non-extinction and non-arising is called Perfectly Pure Nirvāṇa (*pariśuddha-nirvāṇa*). It is quiescent yet constantly illuminating;

when conditions and stimuli arise, it manifests birth, yet this birth is not truly born. When conditions cease, it undergoes extinction, yet this extinction is not truly extinguished. This non-arising and non-extinction is called Skillful Means-Pure Nirvāṇa (*upāya-śuddha-nirvāṇa*).
Non-arising and non-ceasing is called *nirvāṇa*; its full name is *mahāparinirvāṇa*. Translations from antiquity have varied;
while many texts generally adopt the translation "Great Extinction" (*dà mièdù*), the present text adopts the translation "Non-arising and Non-ceasing.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-ṭīkā* quotes the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which states: "*Nir*" means non-arising, and "*vāṇa*" means...
The statement that "neither ceasing nor arising is called Great Nirvana" is precisely this meaning.
However, in the present text, it is clarified that all three types of nirvana are termed "neither arising nor ceasing. Regarding the "true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena":

all phenomena are the provisional (*upāya*), while true reality is the real (*tattva*). To explain this in terms of phenomena and principle: the phenomena of all things constitute the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the middle (*madhya*). To explain this by way of the middle and the two extremes:
all phenomena (*dharmas*) constitute the two extremes, while the true mark is the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Here, we take the fact that all phenomena are themselves the true mark and that the two extremes are themselves the Middle Way to clarify the *pariśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity). Therefore, the *Fahua wenju* states: "The true mark is signless (*animitta*)."
Furthermore, there is neither the mark of birth-and-death nor the mark of nirvāṇa; there is only the mark of the Middle Way as it truly is. Therefore, it is called the "true mark.
Because the nature of the Middle Way is pure and lacks the mark of birth-and-death, it cannot be defiled; this is non-arising.
Because the nature of the Middle Way is pure and lacks the mark of nirvāṇa, it cannot be purified; this is non-extinction. That which is called "perfect purity" is...

The phrase "the perfection of wisdom accomplished through the cultivation of causes" means that it is complete. Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*), it refers to arising and ceasing according to the capacities of beings, being indeterminate;
because it arises and ceases, it is called expedient means. ○ Next, one should understand that what follows below is integrated with what preceded it.
One should know that these three aspects of nirvāṇa—being unborn and undying—are eternal; because they are eternal, they are called bliss; because they are bliss, they are called self;

and because they are self, they are called purity. Since nirvāṇa is thus characterized by eternity, bliss, self, and purity, it possesses the three virtues (triguṇa) which are worthy of honor and respect;
therefore, it is the Three Jewels (triratna), non-dual and without distinction.
Third, following the preceding example for the sake of illustration:
just as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* was used as a metaphor for the three virtues and the Three Jewels, here again the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is used as a metaphor for the three types of nirvāṇa.
III. Explanation of the Text on the Three Bodies (Trikāya) is divided into three parts:

first, the formal explanation. What are the three? What are the bodies? The Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa—these are the three. Because they are aggregates of three kinds of dharmas, they are called "bodies" (kāya).

Specifically, the aggregate of the dharma of principle is called the Dharmakāya; the aggregate of the dharma of wisdom is called the Saṃbhogakāya; and the aggregate of the dharma of merit is called the Nirmāṇakāya.

However, in principle, there is no meaning of gathering or dispersing; it is only by speaking of gathering and dispersing that the true principle first manifests from the initial mind until its ultimate consummation.
The squareness and roundness of the gathering of principle refers to the wisdom that manifests the principle, which begins from the initial mind and culminates in the ultimate.

The squareness and roundness of the gathering of wisdom refers to the gathering of merit, which likewise begins from the initial mind and reaches the ultimate. Therefore, these three are designated as "gatherings" (skandhas).
The three bodies (*trikāya*):

the principle is called the *dharma-kāya*; the unchanging Dharma-principle that responds to causes is called the *saṃbhoga-kāya*; and the wisdom that accords with suchness (*tathatā*) to meet the needs of sentient beings is called the *nirmāṇa-kāya*.

Because it benefits sentient beings through its functional activity and because merit is accomplished through the accumulation of practice, it is termed "merit" (*guṇa*). Therefore, the *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra* states: "It is called the fruit."

Because there is the function of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and transformations to benefit sentient beings, it is called "merit" (*guṇa*); that is, the myriad virtues are what constitute "virtue" (*guṇa*).

Regarding the three clusters of dharmas, all state that they "begin from the initial mind and end at the ultimate," meaning they begin from the first arousal of the bodhicitta and culminate in wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, in the *Miaoxuan*, the explanation of the three bodies (*trikāya*) states: "Profoundly penetrating transgressions..."
The auspicious marks illuminating the ten directions are the *saṃbhogakāya*; the subtle and wondrous *dharmakāya* is the *dharmakāya*;
and the possession of the thirty-two marks is the *nirmāṇakāya*. In the *Fahua Wenju*, this verse is categorized as follows:
the first half-verse clarifies that by upholding the sutra one attains understanding; the subsequent two verses clarify its accomplishment.
One should know that the final line of the second verse cites the Buddha as a witness to prove that upholding the sutra results in liberation;

this liberation is wisdom, and wisdom is the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*). The following two lines clarify the accomplishment of the two bodies; according to the intent of the *Miaoxuan*, this can be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, these two bodies are also called the "birth-body" (*janmakāya*) and the "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*), or the "true" and the "responsive" (*nirmāṇakāya*); here, the "true" is the dharma-body.

"He should immediately manifest" means that the text states: "One who deeply realizes the principle of the *dharmakāya* is fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
Since those of the Two Vehicles possess only emptiness and lack the primary and secondary marks, we know that possessing these marks belongs solely to the *nirmāṇakāya*.

As for the statement that one who deeply realizes the principle of the *dharmakāya* is "fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks," it is like the luminous nature of a mirror manifesting the myriad images.

All manifestations are like a wish-fulfilling jewel that rains down inexhaustible treasures; the manifestation of images raining down treasures serves as a metaphor for the birth-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the response-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which are the provisional (*prajñapti*).

The substance of the mirror and the substance of the bright jewel, along with their light, serve as metaphors for the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the reward-body (*sambhogakāya*), which are both emptiness and the middle way.
Within the wish-fulfilling jewel, when one speaks of its light and its treasure, they are neither identical nor different; this is like the substance of the mirror and its bright images.

Their intent is entirely consistent; yet, those of the Four Ming Temples, being ignorant, take the thirty-two marks of physical perfection to be the marks of the Dharmakāya, and even name them the "Exalted and Extraordinary" (Zhuntè) Reward Body—is this not a grave error?
Next, one should understand that what follows below is integrated with what precedes it.
One should know that the three bodies are all eternal, blissful, self, and pure; they are the three virtues worthy of honor and reverence, which are the Three Jewels;
they are neither born nor extinguished, which is nirvana; they are non-dual and without distinction.

III. Since the following sections apply this principle by analogy, just as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* was used to illustrate the three virtues (*triguṇa*), it is now likewise used to illustrate the three bodies (*trikāya*). IV.
The explanation of the text on the three great vehicles (*trimahāyāna*) is divided into three parts; first, the formal explanation.
What are the three types of bodhi? First, the bodhi of the single true nature (*ekasatya-bodhi*), also called unsurpassed bodhi;
this bodhi takes principle as its path. Second, the bodhi of the two kinds of real wisdom (*dvividha-tattvajñāna-bodhi*), also called pure bodhi;
this bodhi takes wisdom as its path. Third, the bodhi of skillful means (*upāya-bodhi*), also called ultimate bodhi; this bodhi takes skillful adaptation as its path.
"Meeting is the Way.
*Bodhi* is translated here as "Way"; therefore, all three are called "Way. Next, one should understand that what follows below is integrated with what precedes it.
One should know that the three types of enlightenment (trividha-bodhi) are all identical to the three virtues (tri-guṇa)— eternal, blissful, self, and pure— without any duality or distinction.
Since the three virtues have already been illustrated by the analogy of gold,
light, and brightness, one now uses gold, light, and brightness as an analogy for the three types of enlightenment as well.
○ Sixth, the explanation of the text on the three types of *prajñā* is divided into three parts.
First, the formal explanation: What are the three *prajñās*? *Prajñā* is named wisdom (*jñāna*). The *prajñā* of true reality (*dharmatā*) is neither quiescent nor illuminating;

it is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). The *prajñā* of contemplative observation is not illuminating yet illuminates; it is the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*). The *prajñā* of skillful means is neither... [text fragment ends]
Quiescence is itself the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).
Regarding the term *prajñā*, which is translated as "wisdom" (*hui*), in general discourse, "knowledge" (*zhi*) is identical to "wisdom.
However, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "The cause is named *prajñā* and the fruit is named *sarvajñā*," and through such cultivation...
"Wisdom and so forth" refers to wisdom being present in the cause;
if it were said that "calm abiding and insight are the cause, while eye-knowledge and wisdom are the fruit," or "the Tathāgata’s wisdom and so forth," then wisdom would be present in the fruit.
For now, we speak from the perspective of the cause; therefore, it is said that *prajñā* is named "wisdom. It is not non-quiescent, nor is it provisional. It is not—

That which illuminates is not emptiness. "All modes" refers to knowing that all phenomena possess the single characteristic of the mark of quiescence, and being fully cognizant of their various types of activities and appearances.
"Contemplative illumination" means the light of the wisdom of contemplation; it is an illumination that is non-illumination while yet illuminating.
"Omniscience" refers to knowing that all phenomena possess the single characteristic of the mark of quiescence. "Skillful means" is—

The wisdom of the knowledge of the paths of the Buddha-vehicle (mārgajñatā) knows the characteristics of the various paths within the ten dharma-realms, as well as their aspects of delusion and awakening.
Since the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is neither quiescent nor illuminating, one should know that the skillful means of contemplation and illumination are precisely "quiescent yet illuminating.
Next, one should understand that what follows below is integrated with what preceded it.
One should know that the three kinds of *prajñā* are all eternal (*nitya*), blissful (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and pure (*śubha*),
being non-dual and indistinguishable from the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Since the three virtues have already been illustrated by means of the analogy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the three kinds of *prajñā* are likewise illustrated by the analogy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
○ Seventh, the explanation of the three Buddha-natures is divided into three parts.
First, the direct explanation: What are the three Buddha-natures? "Buddha" means awakening; "nature" means that which does not change. That which does not change is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Like gold hidden within the earth, it cannot be destroyed by celestial māras or external paths; this is called the *dharmatā-nature* (true cause) Buddha-nature.

The Buddha-nature as the cause of realization (*jñāna-hetu*) refers to the wisdom of awakening that is neither permanent nor impermanent; this wisdom accords with principle, just as a person who skillfully knows a hidden gold mine.
This wisdom cannot be destroyed and is called the Buddha-nature as the cause of realization.

The Buddha-nature as the condition for realization (*pratyaya-hetu*) refers to all non-permanent and non-impermanent meritorious virtues and roots of goodness that assist the wisdom of awakening to manifest the true nature, just like weeding a field.
Weeding out the weeds and filth to unearth the hidden treasure of gold is called the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditional cause) Buddha-nature.

The Buddha is named "Awakened" (*buddha*) because he possesses the three types of awakening; this is called "unchanging. Furthermore, possessing the three natures, it is the "correct cause" (*samyag-hetu*) which cannot be altered or destroyed.
Since it is described as being neither eternal nor impermanent, its correspondence with the wisdom of awakening—the *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause)—is likewise called "neither... [eternal].

Since the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) is thus neither permanent nor impermanent, how could it not be the case that the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) assists the revealing cause to manifest the reality?

In the previous explanation of the three types of *prajñā*, the essence was clarified through its function; therefore, it was said that they are neither quiescent nor illuminating, yet they are both quiescent and illuminating.

Now, in explaining the three Buddha-natures (*buddha-dhātu*), the essence is clarified through its function; thus, both the contributing and revealing causes are described as being neither permanent nor impermanent.

Regarding the passage on impermanence, such as "like a gold treasury within the earth" and "even until the gold treasury is excavated," this employs the analogy of the gold treasury within the poor woman’s house from the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, saying:
"The 'I' is precisely the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha; all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. This refers to...
My doctrine is that from time immemorial one has been covered by afflictions and thus unable to see [the truth]. It is like this:
within the house of a poor woman there is a great store of genuine gold, yet none of her family members, whether young or old, know of it.
At that time, a certain person skilled in expedient means said to the poor woman, "I will now hire you; you may work for me to weed and clear away [the weeds]."
The woman of impure reputation replied, "I am unable to do so now;
however, if you show me the store of true gold belonging to my son, then I shall quickly act for you. The man replied, "I know the skillful means and can show it to you.
The woman spoke again, "Even the members of my household, great and small, do not know of it themselves; how could you possibly know? The man replied once more:
When he said, "I now know for certain," the woman replied, "I also wish to see it; you may show it to me.
He then dug up the hidden treasure of gold within her house. Upon seeing it, the woman conceived a sense of wonder.
Now, many texts frequently cite this parable to clarify the six stages of realization (*ṣat-avasthā*). Thus, the *Mohe zhiguan* states: "A poor family possesses a hidden treasure..."
One who lacks knowledge is shown the location by a wise teacher and thereby comes to know it; one weeds out the weeds and impurities and digs them up, gradually drawing closer to the treasure.

Once close, the storehouse is opened and the contents are taken in full for use. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains: "The treasure storehouse in the house" refers to the Principle-Identity (*li-ji*);
"the wise teacher shows it" refers to the Name-Identity (*mingzi-ji*); and "weeding out the weeds and impurities" refers to the Practice-Identity (*guanxing-ji*).

Gradually attaining proximity is the "Similar" stage; having attained proximity and opening the treasury is the "Partial-Truth" stage; exhausting the taking and using [of the treasure] is the "Ultimate" stage.

In the present text, the "True Cause" (正因) that draws forth the golden treasury within the earth is the "Principle" stage (理即); the "Enabling Cause" (了因) of awakened wisdom is the "Name-and-Word" stage (名字即);
the "Conditioning Cause" (緣因) of weeding out weeds and digging out the golden treasury is both [the "Nature-inherent" and "Practice"] stages.
As one gradually draws closer [to the fruit], one should contemplate that the stages of practice (*pratipatti*) are identical to the [resultant] state;

thus, the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary) identifies the three aspects of nature (*svabhāva*) as the stage of reality (*tattva*), the three aspects of wisdom (*jñāna*) as the stage of name (*nāman*), and the three aspects of practice as the stages of contemplative practice (*pratipatti*) and semblance (*sādṛśya*). This interpretation accords with the present [text].

When one reaches the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), the three factors of object, wisdom, and practice are fully developed, continuing through to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Since the opening of the *Nidāna* (the *Zang*) and its exhaustive application are not the primary intent here, they are set aside;

therefore, the current text does not mention the "recent opening of the *Nidāna*" or "exhaustively taking and using it" and so forth. Next, one should understand that what follows below is harmonized with what preceded.
One should know that each of the three Buddha-natures is eternally, blissfully, selfhood, and pure, being non-dual and indistinguishable from the three virtues.
Regarding the third [point], the subsequent examples are applied by analogy.

Since the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) was already used as a metaphor for the three virtues (*triguṇa*), the three characters "Golden Light" are now used again as metaphors for the three Buddha-natures (*trividha-buddhadhātu*).
○ Eighth, the explanation of the three consciousnesses consists of three parts: first, the direct explanation.
What are the three consciousnesses? That which is called "cognition" (*vijñāna*) is another name for wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, the *amala-vijñāna* is the ninth, immovable consciousness; if one distinguishes it analytically, it is the Buddha-consciousness. The *ālaya-vijñāna* is the eighth, non-perishing consciousness;
as it still possesses latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) and is conjoined with ignorance (*avidyā*), when distinguished separately, it is the bodhisattva-consciousness.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states that when it resides within the mind of a Bodhisattva, it is called *prajñā*; this is precisely its meaning.

The *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) is the seventh discerning consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*). To revile birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and to long for *nirvāṇa*, distinguishing them as two, is the consciousness of the Two Vehicles;
in the case of a Buddha, it is simply skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). The "waves" are the sixth consciousness of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), which requires no further elaboration.
Furthermore, it is said:

In the initial "Correct Explanation," it states that the term *vijñāna* (consciousness) means "cognitive awareness" (*jue-liao*) and is thus a synonym for wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding this, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) says:
"If, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the eight consciousnesses are transformed to form the four wisdoms, and furthermore, these four wisdoms are subsumed [into one]..."
Regarding the three bodies: the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality;
the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; and the five sensory consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is Done.

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom constitutes the Dharma Body; the Wisdom of Equality constitutes the Enjoyment Body; and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is Done constitutes the Transformation Body. Thus it is wondrous.

The wisdom of observation (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna) pervades the three bodies (*trikāya*). As stated in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on Practice): "Although the treatise masters say that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*), this does not mean that the three consciousnesses are immediately identical to the one mind.
Rather, it is precisely within this one mind that the three wisdoms are fully present. Now, it is clarified that the three consciousnesses are fundamentally one with the one mind;
because these three wisdoms are complete within this very one mind, it is said that "consciousness is named awakening and realization."
This is another name for wisdom. Regarding "amala" and so forth, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) quotes Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha as saying:

"Ādāna is the seventh consciousness; this is called the 'consciousness that clings to a self. Its substance is the nature of delusion, and it serves as the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*). Ālaya is the eighth consciousness;
this is named the 'store-consciousness' (*ālaya-vijñāna*) because it can contain and maintain the seeds of wisdom without losing them. Its substance is non-existent."

The absence of ignorance is the nature of ignorance; this nature is the *jñāna-hetu* (revealing cause). The *amala-vijñāna*, the ninth consciousness, is named the "pure consciousness" and is the *tathatā-hetu* (direct cause).
The Tripitaka Master from Tang did not accept this consciousness, asserting that the ninth is merely a different name for the eighth.
Consequently, the ninth consciousness does not exist in the new translations of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, nor is it mentioned in the texts of the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*.

It is simply that the eighth consciousness corresponds to the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), the seventh to the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*), and the seventh to the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Now, according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, the sixth and seventh are combined to constitute the contributory cause;

this is because within the sixth consciousness there are also the natures of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena which are themselves of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*). This is intended to clarify the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in detail, rather than being the subject of the present discussion, which concerns only the substance of the three consciousnesses.
In principle, the nature (*prakṛti*) is sufficient for the dharmas such as the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Furthermore, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) states:
"Not taking the ninth [stage] is merely one path of the teaching vehicle (*śāsana-mārga*) for correspondence; it is not the same as the present case. Why?

Because in that [teaching vehicle], one abides in the stage of fruition where the three bodies (*trikāya*) remain distinct, whereas here, in the stage of causation, the three bodies are mutually fused; these very three bodies are simply the three virtues.

The three virtues (triguṇa) pertain to the internal, while the three bodies (trikāya) concern the external; since we now follow the perspective of the initial mind which constantly contemplates the three virtues, this meaning cannot be equated with that [other] doctrine.

Furthermore, it is said that the three consciousnesses (trivijñāna) coexist within the principle-mind (li-xin), and that this is a provisional teaching established merely to distinguish between the remote and the near.
Thus, one should know that in the present text, the pairing of the *amala*-consciousness and so forth with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas likewise conforms to the pedagogical framework (*śāsana*).

The *Menquan* (Gate of the Expedient) addresses this by means of the sequential text, clarifying that the three consciousnesses all possess the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*) because they are non-dual and indistinguishable from the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
While the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) does not discuss the sixth consciousness, although the present text mentions it, it states there is no need for further elaboration;
this is because the sixth consciousness merely functions to differentiate various [objects].
Because it is the *dharma*, it shares with the seventh consciousness the status of being a causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*).
The *āmalavijñāna* is called "immovable" (*acala*) because its fundamental nature is pure and cannot be altered. As for *ālaya*, it is called *ālaya*;
"non-extinguished" (*aniruddha*) means that from beginningless time it has never been severed and is eternally without loss or extinction; thus it is called non-extinguished, yet it is not virtuous.

Because they are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they are called "indeterminate" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Regarding the statement that they contain the seeds from which everything arises, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
"Furthermore, the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) associated with all afflictions that adheres to the basis of existence is called 'proclivity' (*anuśaya*);

because it acts as the seed for the arising of all afflictive entanglements (*paryavasthāna*). Furthermore, regarding the conjunction of proclivities with ignorance (*avidyā*): [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] states... [as above].
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Those that flow along are called 'proclivities' (*anuśaya*) because they lie dormant within the continuum;

that is, those that follow the stream abide within the body, increasing the sense of stagnation and attachment. Alternatively, they are called 'proclivities' because they lie dormant within the continuum according to their predominance.

Therefore, the *Śamathavipaśyanā-vidhi* explains that the ignorance associated with both the internal and external realms consists of the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of views and afflictions.

When combined with ignorance, it is called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*); when not so combined, it is called "independent" (*mūla-vijñāna*). Furthermore, the *Xian-shi lun* (Treatise on Manifesting Consciousness) states:

"The *ālaya* is the retributive consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*). Because it is induced by afflictions, it is also called the 'fundamental consciousness' (*mūla-vijñāna*), as it is the basis for all seeds of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
It is also called the 'residential consciousness' (*gṛha-vijñāna*), as it is the locus of all seeds."
Because it is the dwelling place where all seeds are stored and hidden, it is also called the *ālayavijñāna*.

Since this consciousness is exclusively neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*), the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) states: "The nature of ignorance is itself the nature of wisdom. This is said in contrast to *prajñā*;
however, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* is now cited, which says that when it resides in the mind of a bodhisattva, it is called *prajñā*, whereas for those of the two vehicles...
Because one loathes and rejects the three realms, it is called "scorning evil" (*he-ʼo*); because one joyfully admires emptiness and stillness, it is said to be "delighting in" (*xin-xian*).

Thus, the seventh consciousness is specifically correlated with the two vehicles; therefore, it is said that the consciousness of the two vehicles regarding the Buddha is subsumed within the provisional wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
As for *ādāna-vijñāna*, this is translated as "clinging to self. For what reason does one wish to correlate it separately with the two vehicles?

One should know that the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) disparage birth-and-death (saṃsāra) and long for nirvāṇa; even though they have forgotten [the coarse afflictions], their habitual tendencies (vāsanā) still remain.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The subtle consciousness of *ādāna* has its habitual tendencies forming a violent torrent.

Therefore, one knows that the waves also pertain to the seventh [consciousness]. Consequently, it is the habitual tendencies that constitute the grasping at a self, as when one says, "my robe" or "my [self]."

Since the bowl and other objects have already been compared to the waves of the six consciousnesses, it is verified that the seventh consciousness is compared to the wind, and the eighth consciousness, which contains all seeds, is like the great ocean.
The term "awaiting" (*dai*) means "waiting. Regarding the phrase "not awaiting words," there are two meanings:

first, because the six [consciousnesses] and the seventh are together taken as the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*), they do not await [external words]; second, because the six consciousnesses manifest...
Since their practice can be understood, it need not be further explained. Next, one should know that what follows below is integrated with what precedes it.
One should know that each and every one of the three consciousnesses is eternally blissful, self, and pure, being non-dual and indistinguishable from the Three Virtues (triguṇa).
○ Third: The following sections apply analogies by way of precedent.
Having already used the Three Virtues as a metaphor for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, one now uses the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* in turn as a metaphor for the three consciousnesses.
○ Ninth: The explanation of the text on the "Three Paths" is divided into three parts; first, the formal explanation.
What are the three paths? The past ignorance, the present craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—these three branches constitute the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).

The past formations (*saṃskāra*) and the two present branches [craving and grasping] constitute the path of karma (*karma-mārga*). The seven future branches—consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—constitute the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*).
These paths are called "paths" because they enable passage through these three [lifetimes], and they mutually permeate one another from the side of the afflictions.
Affliction (kleśa) leads to karma; from karma comes suffering (duḥkha); and from suffering, one again returns to affliction. Therefore, they are called the "Three Paths.

The Path of Suffering refers to consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling. As the Great Sūtra says: "Between ignorance and feeling, that which lies in the middle is called Buddha-nature.
This middle is the Path of Suffering, yet it is called Buddha-nature because it is designated as the body of birth-and-death (saṃsāra), acting as the basis for dharmas.
To take the body as being like ice turning into water is to mistake the path of afflictions for prajñā, just as one might mistake a finger pointing at firewood for the fire itself.
To take the path of karma— from formative volitions (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*) up to the five immediate transgressions—
as having the characteristic of liberation is like mistaking the binding of a finger for its release.
In the text, the twelve links of dependent origination are first correlated with the three paths;
thus it says that the three links of past ignorance and the present craving and grasping constitute the path of afflictions, while up to the seven [remaining] links constitute the path of suffering.

Next, the names of the three paths are explained, stating that "path" (mārga) signifies that which enables passage. Since ignorance serves as the means for this passage, it is said to proceed from affliction.

Since affliction (*kleśa*) extends to karma and karma extends to the five links beginning with consciousness, it is said that [affliction] proceeds from karma; since suffering extends to the five links beginning with consciousness and consciousness extends to the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), it is said that [suffering] proceeds from suffering.

Furthermore, since [suffering] also extends to the afflictions, if one follows [the logic that] from craving and grasping one proceeds to existence (*bhava*), and from existence one proceeds to birth-and-death (*jāti-maraṇa*), it can be understood by analogy that ignorance (*avidyā*) extends to formations (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, there is no need for further elaboration in the text.
The Path of Suffering is the Dharmakāya; afflictions are Prajñā; fetters and karma are Liberation.
These three paths are the three virtues (*triguṇa*). As stated in the *Yili*: Question: The twelve links of dependent origination are grouped into three paths to correspond to the three virtues.

Since the body of suffering is characterized by material obstruction (*pratigha*), how can it correspond to the Dharmakāya? Answer: This is explained according to the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which involves a reciprocal correspondence. It is not a correspondence based on the physical body.
Therefore, he made this statement regarding the reality of the three bodies (*trikāya*), which have no sequence of before or after.

Now, let us discuss the beginningless wheel of suffering that is boundless, which is neither identical to nor separate from karma and afflictions. Furthermore, within the present text, we shall discuss the conditions (*pratyaya*) based on a single moment of thought;
based on these conditions, we shall discuss the three paths (*trivartman*); and based on these three paths, we shall discuss the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Therefore, the three paths and the three virtues possess no sequential nature; these three causal virtues are never absent at any time.
How could one further ask whether the physical body is obstructive? Having grasped this meaning, the subsequent passage on "harmonization" can be understood.
As for pointing to firewood as fire: if compared to pointing to ice as water or pointing to bondage as liberation, [this is the same].
This is illustrated by the analogy of fire: when sought through its essential nature, fire must depend upon fuel; likewise, wisdom must depend upon afflictions.
Therefore, afflictions are designated as *prajñā* (wisdom), just as fuel is designated as fire. This is because where there is no fuel, there is no fire;
and where there are no afflictions, there is no *prajñā*. Regarding the five immediate [retributions], if one follows from the cause of immediate karma...

It is said that the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are themselves [the result]. If explained from the perspective of the fruit, as the *Nanshan Jieshu* (Nanshan Vinaya Commentary) quotes from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:

first, because they lead to the fruit of immediate rebirth, abandoning the body to be born into retribution; second, because the suffering is uninterrupted, meaning there is no pleasure in the interim;
third, because the time is uninterrupted, being fixed for one *kalpa*; fourth, because life is uninterrupted, not ceasing in the interim; fifth, because the form is—
The intervening space is like that of the Avīci Hell, measuring eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth;

because it is completely filled by one person or many people, the phrase "both" appears in all three passages of the text. The commentary states that the word "both" (lǎng) indicates an absolute necessity of the expression.
Next, from "one should know" onwards, this section is integrated with what precedes it.
One should know that the substance of the three paths is itself the true, eternal, blissful, self, and pure; it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
Regarding "the substance being itself the true," as the *Zhao lun* says: "How distant is the Way? It is true in every encounter.
How distant are the sages? Their substance is itself the divine. The section beginning with "Since the three... applies analogies by following this same principle.

If one perceives these ten dharma-gates— whether as identical or different— they constitute a single dharma-gate that manifests the characteristics of all dharma-gates.
Whether their characteristics of identity or difference are clearly understood, so it is for a hundred dharmas, a thousand dharmas, ten thousand dharmas,
