Gushan says that the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are identical when compared to the Three Jewels (*triratna*), because both are effects;

they are different when compared to the three realms (*tridhātu*), because the latter are causes. He further states that the other three dharmas and so forth should be explained according to this principle. I, however, say this is not so.
One should understand that in the preceding passage, the ten dharmas are each distinct and thus termed "different"; that they are non-dual and without distinction is what is termed "identical."
For example, in the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), regarding the ten profundities and ten gates: although the single principle is the same, the matters of the ten gates are distinct.
This is what is meant by "the inconceivable is eternally unique; though differentiated, it is not differentiated. Thus, it is identical yet distinct;
though identical and though distinct, it is neither identical nor distinct. The meaning is self-evident—why need one laboriously debate this? *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*
To provide further citations:
the *Avataṃsaka* states that a single dharma-gate has immeasurable dharma-gates as its retinue;

the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the incense pellet of the *Gandhavatī*, the pearl within the great jewel of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the single ground from which all arise in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and bathing in the great ocean waters of *Nirvāṇa*—all these express this same meaning.
When a single dharma-gate has immeasurable dharma-gates as its retinue, if they are realized as identical, then both are identical;
if they are distinct, then both are distinct. Since their names and meanings are each unique, the single dharma and the immeasurable dharmas are thus both identical and distinct.
This is why they are termed "identical" or "distinct" when considered in general.
That they do not emerge from the substance means that while the names differ, the essence is identical. Regarding the *śūraṅgama* incense pellet, the Sūtra says:
"If one pounds ten thousand kinds of incense into a pellet, even burning a single particle will fully manifest all the various fragrances. This also serves as proof for both identity and difference.
The rational nature (*li-xing*) is like the pellet; this proves their identity. To observe them as different within the same, and the same within the different, is the contemplation.
The practice is like burning away all phenomena; the sudden arising [of wisdom] is called "being endowed with all vital energies" (*sarva-guṇa-samanvāgata*).

This is a great proof of their difference. Regarding the "jewel wrapped in cloth" from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it says: "If a *maṇi* jewel is wrapped in various colored cloths and placed in water, it changes its color according to the object.
This also serves as a proof for whether they are identical or different. True nature is like the essence of the jewel, while acquired nature is like the cloth that wraps it.

Hearing the teaching is like placing water [in a vessel]; the manifestation through practice is like the appearance of forms. That the rational nature (*dharmatā*) is no different is the "sameness" of this realization;
yet that it can manifest the forms of all phenomena is the "difference" of this realization. Thus, difference is identical with sameness, and sameness is identical with difference.
That which is produced from the single ground of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is without distinction—this is the sameness of this realization. As for the three [aspects] produced...

"Grass and trees" illustrate this distinction between identity and difference: they are identical yet different, and different yet identical. Regarding "bathing in the great ocean of *nirvāṇa*," a sutra states:
"For example, if a person bathes in the great ocean, one should know that this person has already used the waters of all rivers.

In principle, all phenomena are complete within it, just as all river waters are contained within the ocean. To cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is like bathing; to practice the inclusion of all things is like entering the water.

All names are designated as "function"; this also serves as proof that identity and difference are simultaneous. All such [distinctions] arise from the inherent nature (*li-jù*) before there can be phenomenal function (*shi-yòng*).

This is like the analogy of the earth containing both peach and plum seeds; within the reality (*shí*), there is the provisional (*quán*) without distinction, yet the distinction itself conforms to the principle above—reflect upon this accordingly.
Next, the analysis of the text is divided into two parts; first, the question.
Question: If a single dharma is identical to all dharmas, what is the use of other dharmas when one dharma alone has been taught?
Since the three virtues (triguṇa) as a single dharma are already identical to the nine dharmas and all dharmas, the Buddha should have taught only the single dharma of the three virtues;
what is the use of teaching the remaining nine dharmas and so forth? Next, the answer:
Answer: The Buddha teaches to delight all people, for all people, and in the presence of all people, so that all may awaken.
If he were to speak exhaustively, there would be great benefit; even a single teaching can give rise to various understandings.

By reading through various divergent treatises, one comes to know the intent of the wise; thus, by speaking in various ways, he enables everyone to attain understanding, whether through harsh words or gentle speech.
To return to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is precisely the meaning of demonstrating to people the Dharma that is free from conflict and dispute.
The intent of the answer is this: if even a single teaching can cause the arising of various understandings according to the four *siddhāntas*, how much more so when it is taught extensively?
Therefore, one should read all diverse treatises and listen to their various explanations in order to attain every kind of understanding. These are the coarse words.

The term "etc. refers to the citation from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra*) concerning the verses spoken by King Śrīmati upon his realization, which clarifies that although things appear different, they are identical.

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the coarse and the subtle based on ten dharmas: the three paths and the three consciousnesses are considered coarse, while the remaining eight dharmas are considered subtle.
Although coarse and subtle differ, in the ultimate sense there is no differentiation; this is shown to people so that they may be free from contention.
This also clarifies that although things are different, they are identical; thus, there is no contradiction or dispute.

However, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) were fundamentally rejected as being "disputatious dharmas," while the Mahāyāna approach was designated as "non-disputatious.

Here, however, it is simply because there are ten different dharmas that one might fear people would give rise to disputes; therefore, demonstrating that these ten dharmas are non-dual and without distinction is what is called "non-dispute. It is merely this.

It resides in the "Perfect Ear. ○ Third, regarding the "Discrimination of the Ten Sets of Three Dharmas": the preceding text provided the formal explanation, which concerns the characteristics of identity and difference among these ten dharmas;
the present text provides the "discrimination," which concerns the characteristics of depth and shallowness among these ten dharmas.

If one does not distinguish the depth and shallowness of the ten dharmas, how can one discriminate between the Great and Small Vehicles, or the Partial and Perfect? Therefore, [the preceding section]...

This is what is meant by "discriminating between the deep and the shallow," for the intent lies herein. Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "In wishing to explain the 'new' *i*, one must first understand the differing interpretations of others;
only then can one avoid the errors of the 'old' *i*'s horizontal and vertical [confusions], as well as the losses of heterodox sectarian dogmas and arbitrary reckonings.
Thus, even the ash-smearing heretics reckon that Maheśvara is fully endowed with the three qualities (*triguṇa*)."
It is said that the Dharma-body fills the Dharma-realm, the Reward-body dwells in the Heaven of Sovereign Mastery, and the Transformation-body assumes forms according to the six realms;
furthermore, since the various masters of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna have explained the meaning in this way, one must distinguish between the shallow and the deep. Within this, there are two parts;
first, the heading.
Regarding the threefold critical analysis (*liaojian*): first, a critical analysis of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Second, the primary critical analysis of the text, which consists of ten parts. The first part, the critical analysis of the three virtues, consists of three sections. The first section, the critical analysis of the partial teachings, also consists of three parts;
the first of these is the critical analysis of the *piānzàng* (Tripiṭaka) teaching.
If one points to the marks and signs of the Prince’s physical body as the Dharma-body, then the Dharma-body is at the front;
when [the Buddha] was beneath the King of Trees, his clear, untainted wisdom and the thirty-four moments of mind constitute Prajñā, which is in the middle;

and his eighty-fold parinirvāṇa, the cremation of the body, and the non-acceptance of future existence constitute Vimukti, which is at the rear. These are distinct and sequential: at the time of the Dharma-body, there is no Prajñā.
"When there is prajñā, there is no liberation; when there is liberation, there is no prajñā. This Dharma-body [view] treats these three dharmas as distinct entities.
This is the position employed by the Abhidharmikas of the Tripiṭaka schools; none of these three perspectives can be said to possess the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

If one points to the Prince as being the Dharmakāya present before us, this means that the physical body of Prince Siddhārtha during his causal stage—the substance of his sixteen-foot form—is itself the Dharmakāya; therefore, this Dharmakāya is present here among the trees.
Among all these trees, the Bodhi tree is the most supreme, and is thus called the "King of Trees. This clarifies the thirty [aspects] of untainted wisdom.
Regarding the "four equalities of mind" and so forth, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the various afflictions of the lower stages have not been severed at the time of their causes,

and it is only upon reaching the foot of the tree that they are collectively termed the "nine grades of the nine stages of thought-afflictions" (saṃyojana). Therefore, it is said that the stage of a Śrāvaka of the Tripiṭaka is equivalent to that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
as the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) together constitute eighteen [moments], including the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).

The eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*) within the Path constitute sixteen mental moments (*citta*). Combined with the preceding [moments], these total thirty-four mental moments.
According to the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower eight stages have already been severed prior to the initial cultivation of dhyāna;

only the nine grades of afflictions regarding views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *bhāvanā-heya*) remain fully present in the stage of the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Therefore, one severs them using only these thirty-four mental moments.

Regarding the delusions of view and thought in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), because their faculties are superior, one does not further cultivate the [paths] of the lower eight stages.

Although the delusions of the lower eight stages have already been severed, those of the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana* have not yet been severed; however, because these are merely outflowing (*sāsrava*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* does not apply the name "outflowing" to them.
Upon reaching the foot of the King of Trees (*bodhivṛkṣa*), it states that one severs [them] by means of thirty-four moments of mind (*citta*).
The delusions of the three realms are those to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation; therefore, it is only at this time that one attains the untainted state, which is called *prajñā*.
Regarding "not receiving a subsequent body": this present body is indeed the very last.

Since one has attained *nirvāṇa* with no remainder, such that all traces are extinguished and severed, one will not receive a subsequent body. Why? Because if one were to receive a subsequent body, there would be birth.
Since death has now been forever exhausted, there is no further body; these three virtues possess three distinct temporal stages—initial, middle, and final—and are therefore called "different.

Furthermore, even granting the point made in the text—that from the time of the *dharmakāya* onward, when *prajñā* is absent, this explains the characteristic of the granted difference: at the time of liberation, *prajñā* is absent from the *dharmakāya*.
Because the physical body is reduced to ashes, there is no Dharma-body; because wisdom is extinguished, there is no Prajñā.
In the *Zhi guan*, the meanings of the three virtues according to three teachers of the Hīnayāna are cited; the present passage refers to the second of those Hīnayāna teachers.

Thus, the *Zhi guan* states: "First there is the body with its marks and signs; next, one attains the Prajñā of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); finally, the body and wisdom are extinguished."
When one is fully endowed with liberation, there is already the sense of priority, sequence, and hierarchy—comparable, for example, to the three dots of a water character arranged vertically.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "First obtaining that which is excellent" refers to the completion of the hundred kalpas;

"next obtaining the knowledge of the seeds" refers to the thirty-four moments of mind; and "finally extinguishing the knowledge of the body" refers to entering parinirvāṇa at eighty years of age. Since this is already...
This is the meaning of the Abhidharma-piṭaka, Tripiṭaka, and the numerical treatises (saṃkhyā-śāstra) of the Hīnayāna;

therefore, one cannot designate this as the perfect and subtle Three Virtues of the present sutra, and thus it must be distinguished from it. ○ Next, if one points to the realm of emptiness, the following distinguishes the Shared Teaching (pāryāya-yāna).
If one points to the realm of emptiness as the Dharmakāya, it is "originally existent"; if one takes the wisdom that illumines reality as Prajñā, it is "presently existent";
and if one takes the exhaustion of both causal and resultant fetters as Vimukti, it is "to-be-existent.

Furthermore, even if one were to grant these definitions, they are merely what is taught in the common teachings of the Three Vehicles; even those of former generations who investigated and clarified the Mahāyāna would not accept them.

To describe it as "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" refers to the realm of emptiness, which is named the *dharmakāya*. This is distinct from the physical forms of the three *piṭakas*—the bodies adorned with marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*) or the substance of the six-footed form.
Nevertheless, even within the three *piṭakas*, there are instances where the principle of emptiness is indicated as the *dharmakāya*, such as when Subhūti was in the rock cave.

By contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena within the chamber, one attains the vision of the Dharmakāya. Furthermore, the Tripitaka masters indicate that the essence of the marks and signs exists within the causal stage as the Dharmakāya;
once Buddhahood is attained, it is then termed the "Fivefold Dharmakāya. These are: the body of precepts consisting of unconditioned morality (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*);
the body of concentration consisting of untainted meditation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*); the body of wisdom consisting of untainted insight (*anāsrava-prajñā*); and the two kinds of liberation (*vimukti*).
The liberation-body (*vimukti-kāya*) is of two kinds: first, conditioned liberation, which refers to that associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*);

second, unconditioned liberation, which refers to the complete exhaustion of all afflictions without remainder. Furthermore, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) constitutes the liberation-body, while the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) constitutes the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñānadarśana-kāya*).
It should be understood that among the fivefold dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*), the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*) is precisely these [two].
Because it refers to the meaning of the *prajñā* of the mind, it merely points to the substance of the aforementioned marks and signs as the *dharmakāya*.
The wisdom that illuminates reality is the wisdom of non-arising. Regarding the statement that the exhaustion of both the fetters of the "son" (cause) and the "fruit" constitutes liberation:
while in the previous Tripitaka, eighty types of *nirvāṇa* were considered liberation, this [teaching] refers to *nirvāṇa without remainder* as liberation.
The ear severs the afflictions of views and thoughts through thirty-four moments of mind; this is because the "bondage of the child" has already been exhausted.
Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings are bound by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name-and-form binds sentient beings. The *Siṃhanāda* raises an objection:
"If name-and-form constitutes bondage, then all Arhats, who have not yet abandoned name-and-form, should also be bound."
The Bound Buddha said: "Good son, there are two kinds of liberation: first, the severance of the seed (*bīja-viccheda*); second, the severance of the fruit (*phala-viccheda*).
As for the severance of the seed, the various Arhats have already severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the fetters (*saṃyojana*), which have been rotted away;

however, because they have not yet severed the fruit, it is called 'bondage to the fruit. One cannot say that they are bound by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Although the fruit has not yet been severed, it will certainly be severed."
Therefore, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are the "son" of the fruit, and the fruit is the "fruit" of the son;

thus, when the bonds of the son are exhausted, it is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa with remainder), and when the bonds of the fruit are exhausted, it is called *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa without remainder). Nirvāṇa is also termed liberation (*vimukti*).
Regarding the "Shared Teaching of the Three Vehicles," the three vehicles practice the ten stages (*bhūmi*) in common, which applies to this teaching.
Regarding the meaning [of "exploring and clarifying the Mahāyāna"]: that which was used by those who explored and clarified the Mahāyāna in previous generations is stated in the *Miaoxuan* as:

"The old tradition says the *Shelun* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) explores and clarifies the Mahāyāna and explains the meaning of the Bodhisattva; this is not so. The Master himself said: 'I am now precisely clarifying the true meaning within the Tripiṭaka.
As for 'true meaning,' it is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Since this is the Master's own teaching, how could one falsely misrepresent the Master? Thus [it is said].
The *Zhiguan* states: "The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* clarifies that the self and persons are fundamentally non-existent; although phenomena exist, they are floating and void, not truly existent.
Yet, the masters of this treatise did not realize that within the three baskets of the Hīnayāna, the 'emptiness gate' of the *Kośa* refers to phenomena being floating and void.

Consequently, they claimed that this floating and voidness is identical to the Prajñāpāramitā’s 'being like an illusion and like a transformation,' and thus cited the meaning of the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to interpret the *Kośa*."
The treatise [the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*] discusses that what is empty and non-existent is not real, yet it fails to realize that illusory existence differs from such emptiness.

Consequently, this tradition has been passed down such that all claim the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* is "partially compatible" (*fentong*) with the Mahayana; even Master Nanshan asserted that four parts of the treatise are partially compatible with the Mahayana.
However, in the various texts of our own school, none of these views are permitted (and so forth). Therefore, those of previous generations sought out and clarified the Mahayana.

The intent of the *Triyāna-sādhāraṇa-prajñāpāramitā* (the Prajñāpāramitā common to the three vehicles) employed by the followers of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* cannot be described as the perfect and wondrous Three Virtues (*triguṇa*).

Why is this? Even if one follows the proponents of the *Tattvasiddhi*, who claim that the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* probes the depths of the Mahāyāna, it remains nothing more than the *Triyāna-sādhāraṇa-prajñāpāramitā*.
It certainly does not convey the meaning of the *Asādhāraṇa-prajñāpāramitā* (the uncommon Prajñāpāramitā), let alone the fact that the meaning of the *Asādhāraṇa-prajñāpāramitā* is all-pervasive.

The three virtues of the Distinct and Perfect [teachings] in this present sutra are not even the uncommon *prajñāpāramitā* of the Distinct Teaching; how much less could they be the common *prajñāpāramitā* of the Shared Teaching?
If, as in the section on Paramārtha, one distinguishes the Distinct Teaching from the three [lower teachings] below:
If one follows the explanation of the Master Paramārtha, who clarifies that the Dharmakāya possesses four virtues— two each for *prajñā* and *vimukti*—
this has already been cited above according to his text of "Discrimination" (*liaojian*). From this point downward,
the present school refutes [his view].
This is both unconventional and unique; it is elucidated as one path within the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna). One should know that Master Paramārtha used this [approach] exclusively:
he maintained that while the *dharmakāya* may be called "virtue," *prajñā* and *vimukti* cannot be called virtue.
Furthermore, because they do not accord with the immeasurable, profound, and sublime vastness [of the Mahāyāna], they cannot be called the "King of Sūtras."

"Transverse and yet distinct" means that "distinct" is equivalent to "vertical. Because the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), Prajñā, and Liberation differ in the degree of their endowed virtues, they are called "transverse.
Furthermore, it is said that the Dharma-body is inherently existent, Prajñā is presently existent, and Liberation is existentially imminent;
this is further termed "vertical. Since the preceding text already rejected [this view] as being inconsistent with the Perfect and Distinct [teachings], it is not the Distinct [teaching].
The meaning of the "universal penetration" (jiaotongfang) is merely one aspect; to say it is "one aspect" means it is a single direction.
Within the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the meanings and interests of the three virtues (sande)—whether vertical or horizontal—are not uniform. The *Fahua wenju* states:

"The three Tathāgatas of the nature-virtue (xingde) are called 'horizontal,' while the three Tathāgatas of the cultivation-virtue (xiude) are called 'vertical. The sequence of the Dharma-body first, the Reward-body next, and the Response-body last is also [an example of this]."
Although Paramārtha’s exposition of the *satyadvaya* (two truths) deviates from the intent of the Perfect and Distinct Teachings, it is nonetheless subsumed within one path of the Distinct Teaching;

thus, while Paramārtha’s partial application of the two truths deeply contradicts the Perfect meaning, one should know that the Dharma-body may be designated by the four virtues, whereas Prajñā and Vimukti cannot be so designated.
Therefore, it is clear that Paramārtha’s view does not accord with the present sutra.
The Dharma-nature is profound and vast; this King of Sutras is perfectly sublime. ○ Now, following the clarification [of the three virtues], the next section reveals their perfection.
The three virtues clarified here are as explained above: each and every one is endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity. To discuss them extensively, they are immeasurable;
to discuss them in terms of their loftiness, they are exceedingly profound.
This refers to what was explained above in the "Correct Exposition," wherein it was stated that each of the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti possesses the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*).
Furthermore, because this also discusses meanings such as profundity and vastness, the *Zhiguan* states: "Now we clarify that the three virtues are all inconceivable;

why then do you [discuss them] in terms of verticality and horizontality, or identity and difference? This is an explanation based on the "Treasury of Principle" (*li-zang*); herein, the Body is eternal and Wisdom is perfect.
Because all that is severed and possessed is entirely Buddha-dharma, there is no superiority or inferiority;

because the three virtues are not vertically separated yet their characteristics are darkly unified within the single Dharma-realm; because they are not horizontally differentiated by various establishments;

and because they are neither identical as they all converge in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) nor distinct—this is the explanation based on the causes of practice. Because it is one while being three, it is not horizontal; because it is three while being one...
Because it is one, it is not manifold; because it is not three, it is three; because it is three, it is not one; and because it is one, it is not different.
This is an explanation based on the essence and function [of the teaching]. ○ From "If there are those students... onwards, the following three passages refute delusion.
If those practitioners who have heard this king of all sutras, protected by the four Buddhas, do not understand its meaning, they are like oxen and sheep;
their eyes of wisdom are insufficient for discussing the Way.
Failing to realize that the profound and vast *dharmatā* of this present sutra—the king of all sutras—possesses a perfectly wondrous intent, they treat it merely as something small.
Riding upon the understanding of the partial and gradual is like using the eyes of an ox or a sheep; they are insufficient for discussing the perfect, eternal, and wondrous Way.
This is because one who lacks the eye of faith and understanding to discern the shallow and the deep is like an ox or a sheep whose eyes cannot distinguish the cardinal directions.
To exclude the nine lower dharmas, each must be subjected to this same refutation; this text is merely for the purpose of such textual exposition.

This is abbreviated. Next, regarding the analysis of the Three Jewels, it should likewise follow the previous pattern and include both the Exoteric and the Perfect [teachings], though this is also abbreviated in the text;
the subsequent sections should be understood accordingly. This section is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the Tripitaka Teachings (Zàngjiào).

Regarding the discernment of the Three Jewels: if one points to the attainment of the Way under the King of Trees as the Buddha Jewel; the turning of the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing as the Dharma Jewel;
and the conferring of the clear awakening of the eye of wisdom upon the five men, beginning with Kauṇḍinya, as the Saṅgha Jewel—then by virtue of these Three Jewels, they exist even unto this day.
As for those who follow from the perspective of having characteristics (*sanimitta*), this is found within the Āgamas.
The stages of the Three Jewels clarified here are also the application of the Sarvāstivāda school.

Regarding the Four Truths of arising and ceasing, the *Zhiguan* states: "Suffering and its Accumulation are the causes and effects of the mundane; the Path and Cessation are the causes and effects of the supramundane.
Suffering refers to the shifting of the three marks; Accumulation refers to the movement of the four mental states; the Path refers to [the antidote]..."

When that which is being treated is seized and extinguished, existence ceases and returns to non-existence; because both mundane and supramundane phenomena are thus subject to transformation, they are termed "arising and ceasing.
"Turning" (*vartana*) means "transferring" (*parivartana*). This dharma is transferred into the minds of others to cause them to attain awakening.

The term "wheel" (*cakra*) possesses two meanings: first, the sense of "turning," and second, the sense of "crushing" (*piṣaṇa*). By means of the Wheel of the Four Truths, one transfers [the teaching] to others and crushes [their afflictions].

Those fetters and delusions are like the royal wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), which can both destroy and establish; the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) is likewise, destroying the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*) and establishing one in the principle of the Truths (*satya*).
Regarding the five persons, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya: first, Ājñātakauṇḍinya; second, Aśvajit; third, Bhadrika;

fourth, Vairaṭṭīputra; and fifth, Aśvakapunarvasu. As for "the vision, wisdom, clarity, and awakening": this refers to the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering).

The knowledge of the dharma regarding the suffering of the eye is *jñāna* (knowledge); the patience regarding the subsequent inference of suffering is *vidyā* (clarity); and the subsequent inferential knowledge of suffering is *buddhi* (awakening).
This is likewise for the remaining three truths. Because of this, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"He immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī and taught the Dharma to the five bhikṣus; this is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma. At that moment, because the distinct names of the Arhat, Dharma, and Saṅgha came into existence... [the text continues].
Now, beginning from the Sun of the Buddha, down to the present day, there have been carvings in sandalwood, clay sculptures, palm-leaf manuscripts, yellow scrolls, dyed robes, and tonsured heads;
these represent the maintenance of the Three Jewels in the Final Dharma age. Because they are established based upon the Buddha’s Three Jewels, they are called "conformities.
Since their sequences differ, they are likened to a staircase. Next, the Shared Teaching is distinguished.
If one takes the attainment of the Way under the King of Trees as the Buddha Jewel, the teaching of the Four Truths of Non-arising as the Dharma Jewel,
and the two vehicles and bodhisattvas cultivating true non-outflow, severing fetters, and attaining the state of sagehood through the harmony of principle as the Sangha Jewel—
this is what is taught in the common teachings of the Three Vehicles. Those who investigate and clarify the Mahāyāna find that these two types of Three Jewels are both without permanence.
Pleasure, self, and purity.

Within the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the attainment of the Way under the King of Trees constitutes the Buddha Jewel. From the perspective of the Initial [Vehicle], this refers to the Greatly Perceived Buddha at the site of tranquility (the Bodhi tree);

from the perspective of the Distinct and Complete [Vehicles], it refers to the Small-perceived Buddha at the Deer Park, the Buddha of the Tripitaka. Now, the "Shared Buddha" refers precisely to the two [vehicles of] the *Sūtras* (*Dōgyō*).
Because these are phenomena perceived within [the state of meditative concentration], there is no need for the initial formations of two locations to act as an obstacle.

Regarding the Four Truths of Non-arising (*anutpāda*), the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) states: "Suffering has no characteristic of oppression; Accumulation has no characteristic of conjunction; the Path has no characteristic of duality;
and Phenomena are fundamentally non-existent. Now, there is no cessation; all are empty, and thus they are called 'non-arising'. This refers to the Two Vehicles.
When it says "Bodhisattvas cultivating true untaintedness," it means that the three vehicles equally attain the state of sagehood by severing delusions through the path of ineffable discourse.
When it says "the principle and the words are in harmony," this refers to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), which is named after its principle because its delusion regarding the truth is slight.

These two phrases together summarize the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings. If one points to the "Flower King" [Avataṃsaka] and what follows, it subsequently distinguishes the Distinct Teaching (Biéjiào).
If one points to the attainment of Buddhahood upon the lotus pedestal in the World of Flower-King as the Buddha Jewel;

to the immeasurable Four Truths and the *dharma* of the Buddhas, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as the Dharma Jewel; and to the forty-one ranks of sages and saints as the Sangha Jewel—this differs from the previous [explanation].
While it is not a matter of sequential stages, it is likewise not of the same essence (*ekasvabhāva*), nor is it the Three Jewels as illustrated by the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
The Flower-King World is also called the Flower-Treasury World (*kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), as described in the "Flower-Treasury World Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The precious Flower-King Throne is likewise as described in the *Avataṃsaka*. Furthermore, the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* states:
"At the site of the terrace of enlightenment of tranquil extinction, he sat upon the Diamond Flower-King Throne. The old *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The Great Lotus-King Pure World."
The *New Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Sitting upon the pure Buddha-land of the Great Jewel Flower King and the lotus pedestal is also as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "I, now as Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal; having attained enlightenment, I am the Treasure of the Buddhas.

This refers to the Reward-Buddha (saṃbhogakāya) Vairocana. Regarding the "immeasurable Four Truths of the Buddha-dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," this refers to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
It is said that when one discriminates and calculates the aspects of suffering, its origin, the path, and its cessation, each possesses immeasurable characteristics.

As for the "forty-one worthy sages," these consist of the three worthies, the ten sages, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This differs from the former [classification of] the Reward Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*), and differs from the previous two types of Responsive Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*)—the superior and inferior;
the Dharma and Sangha are to be understood accordingly. Although this is not the sequential order of the two preceding stages, it is nonetheless [a valid classification].
If these are of the same essence, how can they again constitute distinct characteristics? This is because, within the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), the Three Jewels are strictly distinct;
furthermore, they are not what is illustrated by the three characters "perfect" (yuan), "wondrous" (miao), and "round" (zhi) in this present sutra.

Following the previous exposition of the Perfect [Teaching], here too it should be stated that the Three Jewels elucidated now—as explained above—each and every one of them possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and likewise, they should be [the ones] subject to refutation.
It is said that if practitioners do not understand this meaning, they will be like cattle, sheep, or those with eyes on their hearts.
Therefore, the Perfect and Sudden Three Jewels are fused and subtle: the Buddha Jewel is like space as a seat, wherein one is accomplished and all are accomplished;
Vairocana, Śākyamuni, and Lokeśvararāja are all pervasive throughout everything, without a single mark of difference. The Dharma Jewel is precisely non-existence.
The Sangha Jewel of the Four Truths begins with the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and concludes at the stage of the "near-to-perfection" (ekajātipratibaddha);
therefore, these Three Jewels are said to be of one essence. Why? Because "Dharma" means non-awakening, while "Buddha" means awakening; the Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Sangha.
How could they be separate entities? One should reflect upon the following eight sets of three dharmas according to this principle.

III. A Threefold Critical Examination of the Three Nirvāṇas. This section also consists of two parts; first, the critical examination of worldly people and heterodox views. Regarding the critical examination of the three nirvāṇas:

if one who is hungry obtains food, one who is ill recovers, one who is in prison is released, or a macaque obtains wine—such as when a *caṇḍāla* brahmin’s belly is full—all these are instances where worldly people satisfy their desires and take this to be nirvāṇa. If...

To calculate that the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the heaven of no-thought (*asaṃjñika*) is *nirvāṇa* is a false view; it is merely a deluded claim that these constitute *nirvāṇa*.
As for those who say that the fulfillment of one's desires constitutes *nirvāṇa*, and so forth: while *nirvāṇa* is a dharma of peace and bliss, the name "peace and bliss" is applied broadly;
therefore, such instances of *nirvāṇa* are not the Great *Nirvāṇa*. Zhanran (Zhang’an) said: "The peace and bliss of *nirvāṇa* extends throughout..."
The "Chapter on Brahma-Conduct in the Ten Dharma Realms" states: "In the cold hells, encountering a warm wind is taken as joy;
in the hot hells, encountering a cold wind is taken as joy. When monkeys obtain wine, they can dance;
when hungry ghosts overcome their hunger and thirst by obtaining food, this is also called nirvana; and when the asuras overcome their fear by finding refuge."
Regarding the basis [of their views]: it is like a poor man finding a treasure-trove or a sick person recovering from illness; such peace and happiness is also called nirvāṇa.
The brahmin Taṇḍi, having eaten his fill, patted his belly and thought: "This very body of mine is nirvāṇa.

This is reckoning the fruit of retribution within the desire realm as nirvāṇa. The seer Ārāḍa attained the concentration of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*); this is reckoning the form realm as [nirvāṇa].
The Dharma is *nirvāṇa*. Udraka Rāmaputra attained the "perceptionless attainment" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); he reckoned the dharmas of the formless realm to be *nirvāṇa*.

As for those who maintain it is the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), they suppress the mind while retaining the body; they claim that because perception is absent, it is actually non-perception, yet in reality, perception remains outside [the practitioner], which others do not recognize and thus reckon as *nirvāṇa*.
If it were not the attainment of non-perception, it would merely be a state where one does not take the preceding sphere of consciousness as an object.

Therefore, it is called "Neither-Perception" (*na-saṃjñā*); and because it does not take the preceding sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as its object, it is called "Neither-Non-Perception" (*na-vi-saṃjñā*).

Although this meditative absorption lacks coarse afflictions, it possesses ten subtle afflictions: first, feeling; second, perception; third, formations; fourth, contact; fifth, volition; sixth, desire;
seventh, resolve; eighth, mindfulness; ninth, concentration; and tenth, wisdom. Outsiders do not recognize this and mistakenly reckon it to be *nirvāṇa*.

If one truly possesses the dark realization [of emptiness] yet remains fully endowed with the accumulation of suffering, and though the three realms of existence are nearing exhaustion, one still falls back into the three miserable paths—how could this be the ultimate peace and bliss of *nirvāṇa*?
[Next,] "If one has much greed" and so forth, serves to distinguish [this teaching] from the preceding three vehicles.

If a person of great lust attains the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as *nirvāṇa*, this is the *nirvāṇa* of one who practices the skillful means of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).

When the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms are exhausted, one realizes *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*); by cremating the body, the ashes and wisdom enter *nirvāṇa without remainder* (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
A Bodhisattva has not yet attained this *nirvāṇa*; this is the second [type] among the two types of analytical dharma (*dharmapravicaya*) within the *Āgamas*.

Regarding "riding upon Nirvana": if the practitioners of the three vehicles equally exhaust both the fetters of cause and fruit, this is the common Nirvana within the Shared Teaching (*paryāya-śāsana*).

If one points to the Middle Way as the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) as "nature-pure Nirvana" (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*), and to the wisdom of the Middle Way as "perfection-pure Nirvana" (*pariniṣpanna-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*), while taking the shared transcendence of worldly conditions—the exhaustion of fuel and the extinction of fire—as "expedient-pure Nirvana" (*upāya-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*), then these three types are distinct from one another.

That which is unrelated is the *nirvāṇa* of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*). If one says that there are only the two types of *nirvāṇa*— the *prakṛti-viśuddhi* (inherently pure) and the *upāya-viśuddhi* (purified through means)—

and does not clarify the *nirvāṇa* of the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*), such that they remain distinct and unharmonized, this is still the Separate Teaching and is not the *nirvāṇa* illustrated in this sutra.

Those with a predominance of greed enter the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), which is one of the five meditative stabilizations (*pañca-viṣkambhanā*) for ordinary persons (*bāla-pṛthagjana*).
By analogy, the principles for the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), and mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) may likewise be understood.

Thus, these ordinary persons serve as the preparatory means (*upāya*) for those who possess the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) among the noble persons (*ārya-pudgala*)—that is, for those on the path to *parinirvāṇa*—because the stage of the ordinary person is precisely the preliminary practice for the noble person.
It may also be said that those who possess great craving attain the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and take this to be *nirvāṇa*;
these are individuals capable of entering among the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), the ordinary people within the *nirvāṇa* discourse. The wording there is abbreviated and general;

taken as a whole, it should include the *nirvāṇa* of the seven stages of worthiness (*saptakṣāntika*) and the preparatory means (*prayoga*). Thus, Zhangan said: "This reckons the provisional methods (*upāya-dharma*) of the two vehicles as *nirvāṇa*."

"Pan" refers to the afflictions of the three realms, which are the afflictions of views and thought. Although the "bondage of the children" has been severed, the remaining "bondage of the fruit" still persists.
"Fen" means to burn; "burning the body" refers to the body of precepts, the body of concentration, and the two bodies of liberation.
"Ashes" refers to the fire of death; the extinction of wisdom is likewise so called, hence it is termed "ash-wisdom. This "ash-wisdom" is none other than prajñā (wisdom).

Furthermore, because both knowledge and vision, as well as the body and wisdom, have been completely exhausted, it is called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*). Zhanran said: "This reckons the fruits of the Two Vehicles as *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the Two Vehicles; however, if we discuss Bodhisattvas, they are merely at the stage of suppressing afflictions.

Since they are identical to ordinary beings in this regard, they do not yet possess the states of "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) or "without remainder. This, then, pertains to the second [category] of the Tripiṭaka of the Āgamas.
Riding upon the teaching of the supernormal power of the ear, the three vehicles equally realize peace and bliss; this is called "common nirvana.

Within the "distinctive teaching" of nirvana, the phrase "the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished" means that the sentient beings' capacity for response is the fuel and the Tathāgata’s adaptation to them is the fire; when the capacity of sentient beings is exhausted, the Sage’s response also ceases.
This is according to the Mahayana perspective. If one follows the Hinayana perspective, the Buddha-body is the fuel and wisdom is the fire.

Because wisdom relies upon the *saṃbhogakāya*, when the body perishes, wisdom is extinguished; this is precisely the meaning of the "extinguishing of the body and extinguishing of wisdom" mentioned in the two preceding teachings.

If one were to say that there are only the two types of *nirvāṇa*—intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and expedient means (*upāya*)—this is merely citing what is said by those of the [Śrāvaka] stages.
Thus, the *Miaoxuan* states: "Those of the stages say there are only intrinsic purity and expedient purity," and our school refutes this as follows:
If that which is accomplished through the cultivation of causes is taken as "expedient purity," then what would "the extinction of fire when the fuel is exhausted" represent?

Now, taking the rational nature (*li-xing*) as the fundamental nature, that which is accomplished through the cultivation of causes constitutes "perfect purity," while the extinction of fire when the fuel is exhausted constitutes "expedient purity.

By classifying these according to the three types of *nirvāṇa*, they correspond respectively to the "nature-purity" (which is the direct cause) and the "perfect purity" (which is the revealing cause).
Regarding the statement that "expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*), the meaning is not clearly understood by those of the Earth school (*Dicheng*).
Because these followers of the Earth school mistakenly take "perfect purity" (*pariśuddhi*) for "expedient purity," they claim that expedient purity is merely what is explained here [in our school].

However, what our school clarifies as perfect purity is precisely what the Earth school calls expedient purity; thus, although the Earth school speaks of expedient means, they still fail to clarify the conditioning cause of *nirvāṇa*.
The *Pán* (Discourse) states that through the purity of expedient conditions, the cause for *nirvāṇa* is such that "the fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.

Since this was not yet explained therein, it is said that [the *Pán*] has not clarified it. Furthermore, although the followers of the *Dì* (Earth) school speak of both innate purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and purity through expedients (*upāya-viśuddhi*), their essence and characteristics are not mutually identical.
Therefore, it is further criticized as being "separate and non-fused," which results in a Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) that possesses two kinds of [purity].

Because it is singular, it is not perfectly sublime. Section Four: A Comparative Analysis of the Three Bodies (*trikāya*). This section consists of three parts. First, the analysis of partial teachings, which is divided into two.

First, the analysis of the *Hīnayāna* (Tripiṭaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings, which is further divided into two. First, the analysis of the Tripiṭaka; second, the analysis of the Shared Teaching.
The text for this is divided into two: first, the formal analysis of the Tripiṭaka and Shared teachings.

Regarding the discernment of the three bodies (*trikāya*): if one takes the Buddha beneath the king of trees as the *dharmakāya* (true body), and the supernatural transformations into monkeys, deer, and horses as the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), yet fails to clarify the three bodies, this is the intention of the Hīnayāna’s analytical method (*prabheda-dharma*).

If one takes the reality inherent in phenomena as the *dharmakāya* and their transformative functions as the *nirmāṇakāya*, yet fails to clarify the three bodies, this belongs to the [Hīnayāna] method of realizing the essence within phenomena (*tattva-dharma*).

It is so. Regarding the term "analysis of substance" (*tǐxī*): in the Tripiṭaka, names are provisional while dharmas are real; one analyzes the reality until it is empty, like breaking a pillar to make it empty.
In the Mahāyāna, both name and reality are provisional, and their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is empty; it is like a mirror-pillar which, from the beginning, was never a pillar.
When one waits for the pillar to cease and then perceives the emptiness, it is that the shadow is itself emptiness—neither arising nor ceasing—and is not the same as the actual pillar.
Thus, taking phenomena as they are to be the True Body (*dharmakāya*) means, as stated in the preceding text, designating the realm of emptiness as the *dharmakāya*.
Taking transformative function as the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) likewise refers to the manifestations of supernatural powers, such as the forms of monkeys, deer, and horses.
Although the application of transformation is thus, the supernatural transformations of the Tripitaka Teaching are merely produced from a single mind based on fundamental dhyāna;
one cannot produce many at once. When the transformer speaks, the transformed entity speaks; when the transformer is silent, the transformed entity is silent.
Since this is so for speech and silence, it is likewise for other gestures and deportment, as these are not spontaneous, true transformations.
Therefore, in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the transformative function (*huayong*) constitutes the response-body (*yingshen*);

this is because it relies on the principle of non-arising (*wushengli*), and by not employing dualistic responses for sentient beings, it causes each sentient being to perceive [the Buddha] differently. Next, the analysis of the text is divided into two parts.
First, regarding the meaning of the question: if it is as stated above—that reality is manifested within phenomena—this is called the True Body (*zhenshen*).

If "the application of transformation" is taken as the "response-body," then the sixteen-foot body attained under the Bodhi tree according to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) would neither be the reality that is identical with phenomena, nor would it be a response-body like the illusory deer or horse. What kind of body, then, would it be categorized as?
The intent of the subsequent answer is that it pertains to both bodies; first, it clarifies that from the perspective of following phenomena, it is explained provisionally as such.
The Buddha’s body of one zhang and six chi beneath the King of Trees is an image corresponding to the human realm; thus, it belongs to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).

In the *Sub-commentary on the Śraddhābalādhāna* (Fǔxíng), quoting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says: "Manifesting in a form of one zhang and six chi is merely a demonstration of being like an upright human.
Or again, he may manifest as a teacher, a parent, a monkey, a deer, a horse, or any other form whatsoever.

Regarding the "images" and so forth, there is another interpretation: previously, for the time being, it was explained by way of provisional accommodation based on phenomena, assigning them to the *saṃbhogakāya* (Response Body).

This current interpretation, however, is the second stage; therefore, they belong to the *dharmakāya* (Truth Body). Within this, first we take as an analogy the union of wisdom and principle within the Mahayana mind of the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles]:
when principle and wisdom merge and the essence is unified, like a lid fitting its box, this constitutes the true *dharmakāya*. Now...

This Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) is likewise thus: it speaks of the substance through its phenomena; although the person is an image, this very phenomenon is the truth, which returns to the same realm as emptiness.
Is this not, therefore, also categorized as the True Body (Zhenshen)?

Thus, in the Shared Teaching, the identity of phenomenon and truth is called the True Body, just as in the Distinct and Complete Teachings, the Middle Wisdom conjoined with the Middle Principle is so named.
It is because it is the Dharma-body alone that this Dharma-body is also called the "True Body" (*satya-kāya*); this refers to the principle within emptiness.
Next, if one relies on the lower [teaching] to distinguish the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*), the Dharma-body is real while the two [other] bodies are not real.
Although to deny them would contradict the Perfect and Separate teachings, to affirm them is also one path of the Separate Teaching; therefore, they are the "True Truth" (*satyārtha*).
This explanation is not the analogy employed here. Next, regarding the subsequent passage that reveals the perfect [teaching], it is divided into two parts.
First, the clarification of the three bodies:
if one says that all three bodies are the true reality, this is the Dharma-body; the wisdom that accords with this reality is the Reward-body; [the wisdom that arises...]
By means of this, the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is the response-body; it is truly that which is emanated by the Real Buddha, entirely real and not false.
As the Great Sūtra says: "The contemplation of impurity is both real and false. To perceive what is not impure as impure is 'false';
its ability to destroy the mind of greed is 'real. The response-body is analogous: because it is not the fundamental essence, it is 'false'; because it can bring benefit, it is 'real. Now...
Because one takes the side of reality and not the side of emptiness, it is said that all three bodies are real; this is what is intended here.
That they are "all real" means that the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* belong to the realm of reality, which is easily understood. As for the *nirmāṇakāya* being real:

because the *nirmāṇakāya* is wisdom that is in profound union with the essence (*tattva*) and is able to give rise to great activity, it is real. Since it is manifested by the Buddha who is real in terms of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, [it is likewise real].
Therefore, the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *dharmakāya* and *vipākakāya* are all real and not false.

Thus, citing the example from the *Mahāyāna Sūtra* regarding the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), it is shown that while one does not take what is not actually impure as being impure—this being a "false" conceptualization—it is nevertheless called "real" because, despite being a conceptualization, it can destroy the mind of desire.
The *saṃbhogakāya* should be understood by this same analogy; it is merely...
Various provisional designations made at random—and so forth—what do they do for me?

Since these provisional designations made according to circumstances are not the fundamental essence, they are called "empty. Nevertheless, because they can benefit all sentient beings, they are also called "real.
Now, we take only the aspect of reality that consists of this benefit, and do not take the various provisional designations which are empty.
For this reason, what was previously stated—that all three bodies are real—is precisely the analogy employed in the present sutra.
Next, the example beginning with "If, furthermore...
illustrates that if one discusses the three bodies in a comprehensive manner, they are all real, all empty, both real and empty, and neither real nor empty.
Regarding the four propositions, Gushan says: "Because the retribution-body and the response-body are the Dharma-body, all three bodies are real;

because the Dharma-body is the retribution-body and the response-body, all three bodies are empty. From the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), the three bodies are relative, forming a "both" (double affirmation);

from the perspective of principle (*li*), the three non-natures are the three natures, forming a "neither" (double negation). Siming says: "In the perfect teaching of the three bodies, to raise one is to possess all three; each has [this quality]."
Regarding the four propositions: the *saṃbhogakāya* is real because it is the true realization; the *nirmāṇakāya* is provisional because it is a conceptual construct;
and the *dharmakāya* is empty because both cessation and illumination are equally present. Thus, the three bodies mutually possess one another, and all four propositions are integrated.

Now, I say this is not so. Why? Because when the three bodies are discussed individually, they are all real. As stated above regarding the first proposition, if the three bodies were all empty and so forth, then the other three propositions would likewise follow.

This can be understood by analogy. Why? Because the ultimate principle is fundamentally devoid of the three bodies; they are merely provisional designations established in accordance with worldly convention.

Are not all three bodies empty? Whether they are both affirmed or both negated, it is simply a matter of the three bodies being simultaneously illuminated and simultaneously extinguished—this is the very emptiness and reality of the three bodies.
○ "One should rely on equality," etc., concludes the preceding meaning.
One should establish four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) for each of the three bodies, as explained in detail elsewhere (*etc.*).
Thus, it should be understood that since the three bodies each pertain to the four propositions, the three bodies are simultaneously [encompassed by] the four propositions.
To say they are "simultaneous" means that each individual body possesses all four propositions. This meaning is difficult to perceive; therefore, I shall explain it further. For now:

Regarding the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) applied to the Dharma-body: the ultimate truth that is unchanging is the reality of the Dharma-body; its provisional establishment in accordance with the world is the emptiness of the Dharma-body;
the third proposition is the simultaneous illumination of both; and the fourth proposition is the simultaneous negation of both.

Since this is the case for the four propositions concerning the Dharma-body, the same applies to the four propositions for the Reward-body and the Response-body; therefore, it is said that one should treat them according to the three bodies.
This also forms four propositions. Why? Since the text states that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not the fundamental essence, it is "empty" (provisional).

One should know that all three bodies are provisionally established and are therefore empty because they are not the fundamental essence. People do not see this and merely busy themselves with textual records (*yǔwénjì*).
(As indicated by "and so forth" in the separate record, the notes below state "and so forth," for example, as in the *Fahua wénjù* [Commentary on the Lotus Sutra], which says "four...")

Having already explained the meaning through these propositions, for those who have not yet understood, one further analyzes by means of the four propositions—such as permanence and so forth—first treating them separately and then collectively.
Regarding the separate treatment: the Dharma-body is neither permanent nor impermanent; the Reward-body is permanent;
the Response-body is both permanent and impermanent; and from the Vajra-mind [of the Buddha] down to ordinary beings, it is impermanent.
Regarding the term "also comprehensive" (*tōng*): it refers to a general, all-encompassing exposition stating that each and every Tathāgata is fully endowed with the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).

One should know that this passage provides a general, all-encompassing exposition that each and every Tathāgata possesses all four propositions; this may be used as an analogy for the meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*) in the present text, wherein each is likewise treated according to the four propositions.

Why is this? Because reality (*shi*) is itself permanence (*chang*), while emptiness (*xu*) is impermanence (*wuchang*); thus, there is both [permanence and impermanence] together, as well as neither [permanence nor impermanence].

This can be understood through reflection. ○ Question: Regarding the three characters [below], there are three instances where the illustrative text is applied according to the same principle; this is divided into two parts: first, the question, and second, the answer.
The first part [the question] is further divided into two: first, the formal answer, which is again divided into two: first, clarifying the meaning.
Question: May the three characters be used as metaphors for the three bodies (trikāya), or may they also metaphorically represent one body, two bodies, four bodies, or no body? Answer:

The Buddha responds to conditions by naming the sūtra with three characters; thus, commentators provide explanations in terms of the three bodies. However, if one grasps the underlying meaning, what fault is there in providing explanations in terms of four, three, two, or one, or even no meaning at all?
The Buddha, responding to the specific capacities of a certain class of beings, gave this sutra its distinct title using the three characters *Jin-guang-ming* (Golden Light).
Those who explain its meaning take these three characters as metaphors for the Three Bodies (*trikāya*) and interpret them accordingly.

If they may be used as metaphors for the intent of the Three Bodies, they could likewise be applied by analogy to four, two, one, or the peerless [Bodies]. Furthermore, it is said that the number "three" is used in contrast to...
The phrase "the former cites both" refers to those who specialize in exegesis; that is, families of scholars who interpret the meaning. This is also as stated in the subsequent text:

"The preceding citations of analogies are mostly examples of inferential reasoning based on meaning. Furthermore, regarding the question "what fault is there?", since inferential reasoning is unobstructed, what transgression could there be?
○ Regarding the phrase "all such texts exist within the lower scriptures," this next indicates the consistency of the textual evidence.
The text is found throughout the following scriptures. If one posits four bodies (*kāya*), the New Translation states that Śākyamuni is able to manifest various forms;
this then distinguishes the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body), making four bodies.

If one posits three bodies, there is the "Chapter on the Distinction of the Three Bodies" which specifically discusses their meaning. If one posits two bodies, the Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) remains as...
If space manifests forms in response to objects like the moon reflected in water, and if it were to manifest as a single body, the New Edition states:

"All Buddhas take the True Dharma as their body. If it were to be without a body, the Tathāgata’s sphere of activity would be as pure as space, yet he further enters the Great City of Sublime Tranquility;
within this space, there is no numerical count of three—this is what is meant by being "without a body."
This passage is not only consistent in meaning, but because its exact wording exists throughout the Buddhist scriptures, Paramārtha’s new translation states:
"The various manifestations of Śākyamuni are called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). It may also be understood in this way regarding the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Because he emerges from within [the Dharmakāya] to manifest as a response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is said that he "emerges as a responsive transformation. To appear identical [to sentient beings] from beginning to end is called "responsive" (*ying*);
to suddenly exist where there was previously nothing is "transformation" (*hua*). If one were not to distinguish them, the responsive body would be identical to the transformation body;

therefore, the new edition refers to it as the "transformation body" (*huashen*). Furthermore, the statement regarding the "hundreds of thousands of millions of transformation bodies" also carries this same meaning. Thus, regarding the Śākya lineage...
Among the various manifestations, the opening section concerning the "Responsive Transformation" (nirmāṇakāya) refers to the text of the four bodies (*catur-kāya*).
The "Discrimination of the Three Bodies" chapter likewise refers to the new translation. As for those who specialize in its meaning, it concerns the doctrine of the three bodies.
As previously recorded in full, the *Zhi guan fu xing* quotes the scriptural passage from that sutra regarding the two bodies; this refers to the current sutra translated by Dharmakṣema.

The passage "the one body is no body" can be understood from its text. Now, since the *Sūtra on the Heavenly King Praising the Buddha* states that the Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is like empty space, how can those who study the Four Ming [Commentaries] arbitrarily claim that the essential substance of the *dharmakāya* possesses distinct marks (*lakṣaṇa*)?
Both the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuan Yi* and the *Wenju* judge that when the Dragon Girl spoke the verse praising the Buddha, she was referring to the thirty-two marks of physical form.
Question: Why do you not consider that which is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body)?
If the *saṃbhogakāya* is defined by its possession of marks, why does the text of the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter state that the thirty-two marks are the *dharmakāya*? Answer:

This is because the text is interpreted here in terms of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) for the sake of convenience. Why? Because all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*) is the virtue of *prajñā* (wisdom), and true cessation (*nirodha*)... [is the virtue of *dharma*].

Because it possesses the virtue of liberation, it is called the Dharma-body by virtue of its completeness. Although the Dharma-body is characterized by this completeness, one must understand its underlying intent.
What is that intent? It is that the thirty-two marks are themselves the Dharma-body;

since even the signless wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is not [the ultimate], how much less so the marked forms of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body)? When explained in terms of the Middle and the Extremes, this is the Dharma-body.

Regarding the "neither of the two" (ubhayābhāva) in terms of both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*): because the *dharmakāya* is without marks (*animitta*), one speaks of reaching the realization that marks are themselves non-marks.

If one were to take the thirty-two marks directly as the *dharmakāya* without discussing the realization that marks are non-marks, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* would denounce this as a heterodox path, and the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* would identify it as delusion.
Is it not evident from this? The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni is named Vairocana, pervading all places.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "This body of mine is now the Dharma-body. The *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"To praise the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is to praise the Dharma-body; therefore, the thirty-two marks are called the Dharma-body. This is indeed so.
Reaching the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is precisely the characteristic of the dharma-body (dharmakāya), which is itself signless (animitta).

Therefore, it is said that since the Buddha-eye is the substance of the four eyes, one should know that the four eyes are themselves the characteristics of the dharma-body; thus, by seeking these characteristics, one perceives the signless.

How much more so for the "characteristic of the signless," which is the supreme among all characteristics! Please consult the *Guangjing* (Commentary on the Record) to dispel [doubts] regarding the term "signless."

If worldly people can deeply penetrate such an intention regarding the discourse on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then the texts and meanings of all the various schools within a single tradition will be fully understood.

This is truly because of the principle of "one thread running through" (*ekena sūtreṇa sarvam anupraviśati*); it does not require the exhaustive presentation of two separate examples. As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:

"The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty and quiescent; this emptiness of nature is itself the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The nature of phenomena is fundamentally pure, like space."
"All dharmas with marks are without marks; this is the true body of the Buddha. Master Sheng said, "The Dharma-body is without color.

The *Sūtra on Contemplating the Buddha* Commentary says, "The Dharma-body has no image. How can one fail to reflect upon such authoritative sayings and yet rashly claim that the marks of the Dharma-body are perfectly manifest?
If the marks of the Dharma-body were indeed perfectly manifest, then the Reward-body and the Response-body would be identical to it.
Why say that the three bodies do not all possess marks? To advance or retreat from this position is equally untenable, leaving nothing by which they may be named.

Therefore, one must know that the fusion and subtlety of the three bodies do not fall outside the four propositions. Why is this? If the three bodies are maintained as distinct: the Dharma-body is definitively without marks;

the Reward-body encompasses both meanings [of having and lacking marks]; and the Response and Transformation bodies are definitively with marks. If, however, their marks are identical, then they are all equally marked.
Both are without marks (*animitta*). If one follows only the principle (*li*), it is neither mark nor without-mark;

if phenomena (*shi*) and principle are held in relation to one another, then no-mark is precisely mark, and mark is precisely no-mark. When the mind penetrates this wondrous accord, all contentious arguments fall away.

Since this is the case for bodily marks (*kāyalakṣaṇa*), the same applies by analogy to speech and silence. (etc. Question: If one cites the Four Heavenly Kings praising the Buddha’s Dharma-body as being like empty space, Master Jingxi—
That statement does not mean that the great void is called the Perfect Buddha. The Master’s answer to this question is excellent;

it is capable of dispelling a multitude of doubts, as is fully explained in the *Commentary on the Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* (*Shi wu lian jing shu*) and the *Record of Rebirth* (*Wang sheng ji*).

It is also clarified in the *New Record of the Words and Phrases of the Present Sutra* (*Jin jing wen ju xin ji*) within the explanation of the verses of praise by the Four Heavenly Kings (and so forth). Question: If that is so, [the following] next distinguishes the application of the analogy regarding expansion and contraction.
The text consists of two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.
First, the question: If that is so, how can the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* be used as an analogy for the four bodies, the two bodies, the one body, and the bodiless?
This is what is being asked. Next, the answer.

Answer: If one uses the meaning of the name as an analogy for expansion and contraction, it is so because of that meaning. If one uses it as an analogy for the four bodies (*kāya*), one takes the radiant flames above the golden light;
the text says, "The golden light shines brilliantly," and this is the passage illustrating the four bodies. If one uses it as an analogy for the three bodies, it is exactly as employed [in the text].
If one uses it as an analogy for the two bodies, the gold is the primary essence (*svabhāva-kāya*) and the radiance is merely its merit (*guṇa*).

One can use this as an analogy, though it is like comparing a single body; however, taking only the gold as the primary analogy is insufficient, for the radiance is merely a secondary detail and not the primary subject of discussion.
If one were to use the "bodyless" as an analogy, then the supreme treasure would take non-attachment as its gold—just as Yang Chen’s "four knowledges" likewise took non-attachment as its gold.
Now, by using the supreme treasure of the world to illustrate the supreme treasure that transcends the world.
"Principle" (*li*) refers to the thorough convergence of words and meanings.
In the response, it says, "using meaning to name the metaphor": since the nominal tone of "name" (*mingzi*) implies using a metaphor to approximate the Dharma, one uses meaning to name the metaphor.
Because one uses meaning to name the metaphor, the expansion or contraction of that metaphor likewise depends upon meaning.
Therefore it is said that "expansion and contraction depend upon the meaning. "Expansion and contraction" refers to advancing and retreating, increasing and decreasing.
"Yù (yú liù qiè) yào (yǐ zhuó qiè)" refers to the flames of light; it also means "abundant. The character "yàn" should be written as "yàn.
The flames of "yù-yào" are precisely the "huàng-yào" (resplendent glare). Thus, the citation for proof says: "The golden light is resplendent, yù-yào and huàng-yào, suddenly..."

That which exists suddenly and cannot be compared is the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). If one were to compare it to the three bodies (*trikāya*), it would be like what was used in the preceding passage above.
If one were to compare it to the two bodies, as in the phrase "gold is the true essence," this is also like the other person cited in the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), who said:
"Within the ore-stone there is gold; the essence of gold is neither radiance nor brightness, yet it does not hinder [the presence of light]."

Discussing the internal and external applications of the Dharma-nature through the analogy of gold: the Dharma-nature itself is neither the thesis nor the power, yet both thesis and power arise based upon the Dharma-nature;

thus we know that the essence of gold can be used as an analogy for the True Body (*dharmakāya*). Since its radiance is a functional capacity inherent in that essence, possessing both internal and external applications, it can be used as an analogy for the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
If one uses the analogy of a single body, taking only the primary essence, the meaning will be clear. This is the analogy.

Regarding the citation of Yang Zhen’s "Four Knowledges" (*sì zhī*) within the section on the bodiless [spirits]: the *Hou Han Shu*, in the Biographies (*Liezhuan*), states that Yang Zhen, styled Boyi, was a native of Huayin in Hongnong.
At the age of fifty, he finally began his official career at the provincial and commandery levels.

When the Grand Marshal Deng Zhi heard of his virtue, he recommended him for the rank of *Mocaicai* (Man of Outstanding Talent). After four promotions, he served as the Inspector of Jingzhou and subsequently as the Governor of Donglai. As he was about to depart...

While traveling on the county road through Changyi, Cui Zhun encountered Wang Mi, who had previously been recommended as a "Talent of Jingzhou. Wang Mi was serving as the Magistrate of Changyi and came to pay his respects.
When night fell, he placed ten *jin* of gold in his robe to present to Zhun. Zhun said, "It is because you, my old friend, know me, while I do not know you, my old friend;
why is this? Wang Mi replied, "It is a time of twilight and night; there is no one here who knows. Zhun said, "Heaven knows, the spirits know, and I know."
When his son asked what he meant by "ignorance," Zhen was secretly ashamed and left. Later, he served as the Governor of Zhuo Commandery;
by nature he was upright and incorruptible, refusing private audiences for favors. His descendants always ate vegetarian food and traveled on foot.

When old friends and elders wished to help him establish a family estate, Zhen refused, saying, "I wish that future generations may call me a 'pure and honest official,' and that my descendants shall live by this reputation."
Is this not a profound legacy? Thus, Yang Zhen’s integrity, incorruptibility, and purity are the supreme treasures of the nation;

therefore, non-greed is treated as gold. By using the gold of non-greed—the supreme treasure of the mundane world—to metaphorically illustrate the formless and most wondrous principle of the supramundane, the text and its meaning are brought into even greater harmony. (Section Five)
Distinguishing the Three Mahāyānas:

Regarding the distinction between the three Mahāyānas, if one considers the Mahāyāna of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) based on causes and conditions, this is still the same in meaning though differing in name for the three types of persons.
If one considers the three types of persons who equally employ non-arising (anutpāda) to sever afflictions, they are all riding upon the same vehicle.

The first is the Middle Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). If the principles are attained accordingly, yet the essential natures and characteristics of the three vehicles remain distinct and different, this is the Middle Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
These three types are all subsumed under the "vehicle for attainment" (*de-cheng*).
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Elephant Vehicle is clarified as being added to the three to make four; the sheep, deer, and ox vehicles are subsumed within the vehicle for attainment.
The "elephant vehicle" (hastiyāna) is precisely the "vehicle of principle" (tathatāyāna), which refers to the three vehicles as clarified here. In the *Avataṃsaka*, four vehicles are explained;
the three vehicles are also subsumed within the "attainment vehicle" (prāptiyāna). The "Buddha vehicle" (buddhayāna) is precisely the meaning of the present three vehicles.

If one considers the six *pāramitās* in relation to causes and conditions, such that the names of the three persons differ while their meanings remain the same, this distinguishes them from the *Tripitaka* Teaching.
Thus, the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) states: "The three causes are greatly different, while the three fruits are slightly the same. The *Shiqian* (The Sub-commentary) explains:

"Because the truths (*satya*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and perfections (*pāramitā*) differ, the causes are greatly different; because all three vehicles equally sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), the fruits are slightly the same. Regarding the truths and conditions: [the text continues as above].

Since these represent different ways of opening and closing [the teaching], this text now mentions only the *nidāna* (causes and conditions) and the six *pāramitās*, which thereby encompass the Four Noble Truths.

In the *Fahua wenju*, the Four Noble Truths of the śrāvaka are designated as "Small," while the *nidāna* of the pratyekabuddha and the six *pāramitās* of the bodhisattva are designated as "Middle" and "Great" respectively.
