As for "based on the essence itself," various texts of this school clarify that when referring to the essence itself, it must necessarily be contrasted with its basis; thus, the *Wenju* states:

The *Jiming fangbian pin ti* (The Substance of the Chapter on the Clarification of Expedient Means) states: "As for what is called 'substance' (*ti*), does it refer to that which is taken as the basis (*āśraya*), or does it refer to the substance itself?
If one takes that which is the basis, then it is the provisional (*upāya*) that constitutes the substance;

if one takes the substance itself, then it is the real (*bhūta*) that constitutes the substance. These two meanings are distinct yet inseparable, and though they blend, they do not become confused; therefore..."
The distinction is made between that which is provisional yet real in its essence, and that which is real yet provisional in its very substance.

Thus, the principle within the emptiness of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is that upon which phenomena depend and that which serves as the substance for names; the functional activities of all phenomena are fundamentally inherent within this principle.
"That which accords with the substance" refers to the self, the source, and the fundamental nature of all phenomena. This is the [principle] existing upon the phenomena of all things.
This is because names arise from the fact that the reality of the self-nature is inherently complete. Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"In the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there are real names and meanings"—this is precisely that meaning.

Since the ultimate truth already possesses both phenomenal function and names, the names for the phenomenal functions of all dharmas are fundamentally not of the conventional world; they arise entirely from what is intrinsically complete within the principle (li). Thus...

Regarding the three characters of the specific title of this sutra: if one attaches them to the main text, the "Introductory Chapter" states, "This is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*," whereby our Buddha first pointed to the matter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and established the name of the three-character specific title.

However, if one considers it according to its essential nature, one must know that the three characters of the specific title established by pointing to a particular matter are, in their essence, the Dharma itself.

That which is inherently possessed by the essence of nature—the name for the functional activity intrinsically present within the true Dharma-nature of our Buddha-Sages—is established as the conventional title "Suvarṇaprabhāsottama" (Golden Light).
One should know that within the emptiness of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the substance vanishes and is extinguished;
being signless and nameless, the *Wenju* (Words and Phrases) states: "As for its substance, it is real."
"Characteristics have no differentiation. Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) states: "Names lack the power to summon things, and things lack the reality that responds to names;

this is precisely the meaning of 'no-characteristic' within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) explains: "Dharmas are fundamentally nameless, and names are merely provisional and lack reality;
therefore it is said that names lack the power to summon things. Since the essence and nature of things are empty, there is nothing to respond."
The provisional name and the real name are both non-existent; it is merely a matter of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Although the essential substance of the ultimate truth is indeed nameless, it inherently possesses the names of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Therefore, the sages, conforming to the conventional, provisional names inherently present in the ultimate truth, established designations for functional utility. Thus, the *Wenju* [states]:...

Regarding the application [of these terms], the established principles differ in their gradations; furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "In terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is no name by which the Dharma could be manifested;
therefore, the first treatise explains the names. The *Shiqian* commentary explains: "Since this treatise now discusses conventional truth, it is necessary to distinguish the names;
thus, the *Xuan* and the *Qian* speak of the primary meaning, the true reality (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the fundamental essence, and for this reason it is so called."

"Nameless and signless"—the present text discusses the names for the inherent phenomenal functions within the True Truth (*tattva*). Therefore, it is said that the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) possesses real names and meanings.
One must understand that while these are inherently endowed (*li-jù*), they are the provisional designations of the body and virtues of the *Vajrasūci*;
being nameless and signless, they are the nature and measure of the body of the *Vajrasūci*, which is both emptiness and the Middle Way. This is thus...

Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), all phenomena are eternally present as provisional entities and functions; that these provisional phenomena are conventionally permanent is precisely where the integration of principle and phenomenon within the emptiness of intrinsic nature resides.

Now, in this passage, it is stated only that "in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) there are real names and meanings," without mentioning that "in the ultimate truth there are no names or marks.
This is because the preceding passage has already explained the general and specific [meanings].

It is said that this is because, in principle, there are no names. Thus, although the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary) merely states that the True Truth (*satyadharma*) is nameless, it would logically follow that one should further state that it inherently possesses all names;
for throughout the various passages of the *Xuánqiān*, both preceding and following, the inherent presence of principle (*lǐjù*) is extensively elucidated.
Therefore, in the section explaining "names," it was omitted for brevity. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation of the *Miaofa* (Wonderful Dharma):
Although it is not explicitly stated therein that the principle (*li*) inherently possesses all names, the *Lotus Sūtra* itself says: "The Lotus derives its name from its very substance.

This is the principle of the Dharma (*dharmatā*) governing phenomena. While the present text speaks only of the True Truth (*satyadharma*) as being fundamentally endowed with both name and reality, the preceding text has already stated that the essential body of the principle is originally devoid of names.
Thus, [the meaning of] the *Xuanzan* (Profound Commentary) and the present [text]...
To summarize these points: the essence of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is nameless, yet it eternally possesses conventional, provisional names.

When the sages look up to this ultimate truth, they find it to be nameless while simultaneously possessing all names; thus, they establish names for the functional activities of various phenomena in accordance with worldly convention.
Therefore, one should know that if one is biasedly attached to the idea that the ultimate truth is merely nameless—
To say that names merely obtain the fundamental substance (*tattva*) of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) while losing its inherent qualities is an error;

conversely, to insist that names are merely inherently present within the principle (*li*), thereby obtaining its inherent qualities while losing the fundamental substance of ultimate truth, is likewise an error.
Therefore, the present text refutes the ancient masters' claim that ultimate truth is nameless and establishes that ultimate truth possesses names.
The existence of names in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is precisely due to this person’s failure to perceive it;

they merely cling to the literal text, asserting that names exist in the ultimate truth while refusing to admit that, in the ultimate sense, names and marks are fundamentally non-existent. They then immediately raise an objection, saying:
"If you claim that the ultimate truth has no names or marks, how does this differ from the ancient masters? Alas, what a pity! This is a profound error. Why is this so? If one... [text continues]
Regarding the statement that "the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is nameless," the *Wenqu* (Textual Commentary) says, "The principle is without names and characters.

Furthermore, the *Xuānqiān* (Profound Pivot) says, "The ultimate truth is nameless. Is this not the teaching of the ancient masters—the principle being without names and characters as stated in the *Wenqu*, and the ultimate truth being nameless as stated in the *Xuānqiān*—and not the doctrine of our own school?
The *Wénjù Jì* (Record of the Textual Commentary) states: "Nature is fundamentally without [name]."
It is called "endowed with all names" because it speaks without speaking; this is precisely what constitutes the teaching, and this is the intended meaning.

Therefore, one must understand that what is stated in the present text—looking upward toward the True Dharma and looking downward at conventional designations—necessarily supports the preceding principle.
Since names are the principle and the principle is named by names, the meaning of the distinction between the previous principle-teaching and the present True and Conventional is identical. If...
If it were not so, why would the *Wenju ji* (Record of the Phrases) state: "The nature is originally nameless, yet it is fully endowed with all names;
though there is nothing to be said, one speaks, and speaking necessarily constitutes the teaching"?

Therefore, we know that since the preceding passage clarifies the distinction of the teaching (*jiao*), and those three characters of the distinct title are already established as names, the present establishment of the conventional designation (*suhao*) is likewise a distinct title: *Jinguangming* (Golden Light). Thus, [it is] profound.

The divination slip states, "Discerning names according to worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is precisely this meaning. If this were not so, would the teaching in the preceding passage not be distinct from the conventional designation in the present passage?
Therefore, one should know that if one grasps this principle, the subsequent text can be explained as clearly as viewing fruit in the palm of one's hand;
if one fails to see this meaning, one will inevitably lose the correct direction—not only will one be confused regarding the intent of the present passage, but one will also fail to grasp it.

This also deviates from the intent of the *Xuānqiān* (Profound Commentary). Siming states: "The three characters 'dāng' (appropriate), 'zhǔ' (master), and 'dāng' (appropriate) are direct names for the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena);

therefore, it is said that the essence itself is appropriate (*dāngtǐ*). Now I ask: if these are direct names for the *dharmatā* and are thus called the "essence itself," why does the subsequent text say, "taking the dharma itself as a metaphor"?
Furthermore, Siming says: "The previous [explanation] was an attachment to the text to explain the name and its function."

Regarding the two terms "directly designating the essence" (*dangti*) and "attached to the text" (*futext*): "directly designating the essence" refers to a name that directly invokes the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) by means of its principle;
"attached to the text" merely establishes a name by pointing to a specific phenomenon.

Now, concerning the title of this specific work, which consists of only three characters, how can one distinguish between these two types of names—those that designate a phenomenon and those that designate a principle? Therefore, it is necessary to understand "directly designating the essence."
The name "the essence of principle possessing the function of phenomena" is simply a name that attaches to the text to point toward the phenomena;

however, whereas previously it was directly attached to what is produced by the scriptural text, here it clarifies that these are inherently present within the essence of principle. Thus, there is a distinction between "attaching to the text" and "being the essence itself.
Although these two paths are divided, their intent follows the same track; therefore, in the subsequent analysis, one simply uses "attaching to the text" as the counterpart.

The third analogy regarding the question and answer is precisely for this reason; it does not mean that the name for the functional application attached to the text differs from the name for the principle inherent in the substance itself.
○ A certain master says: "The subsequent explanation of the text is divided into two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the critical examination.
The first part is further divided into two: first, clarifying the purpose of the introduction; this section is again divided into two, the first of which raises [the point]..."

He said: "Some masters claim that in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) there are no names, while in the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) there are names; one relies on names within the nameless to provisionally discuss the ultimate through the mundane.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: 'Within the absence of names and marks, one speaks of names and marks by way of provisional designation.'"

It should be understood that this passage is entirely identical to the *Xuanji* (Profound Commentary), which explains that within the *miao-fa* (wondrous Dharma), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is nameless while the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) possesses names;

furthermore, it corresponds to the "Initial Clarification of the Great Meaning" within the section on the characteristics of the teachings (*jiao-xiang*), which states: "The Buddha, within the realm of namelessness and formlessness, provisionally employs names and forms to teach.
This was because the ancient masters did not realize that although the essence of nature (*xing-ti*) is fundamentally nameless, it inherently encompasses all phenomena through worldly convention."

Because it is so named, the subsequent text now refutes it. If this were not the case, why would the present text contradict the ancient masters by asserting that the True Truth (paramārtha-satya) is nameless while the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya) has names?

Furthermore, why would the *Xuanqi* (Profound Commentary) employ the position that the True Truth is nameless while the Worldly Truth has names, and additionally utilize the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* to explain that among names and characteristics, there are "provisional names and characteristics"? From this, we know the nature [of the teaching].

The full possession of all dharmas arises entirely from the fact that their substantial essence is extinguished; they appear like images in a mirror, which occurs solely because the mirror’s surface is bright. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states:
"One is able to realize that deluded thoughts possess not even a single mark of difference or identity. By penetrating this signlessness, one possesses the entirety of the mind.

Only when the three thousand [realms] are fully present can one then illuminate the mutual identity of the one and the many. Since these are inherently possessed by nature, and since that essential nature is itself extinguished," so forth.
If the essential nature (xingti) did not inherently possess all real conventional phenomena and their provisional functions, how would it differ from a *sphāṭika* gem, which cannot rain down jewels?
Therefore, the ancient masters spoke only of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), wherein the fundamental substance is extinguished and beyond name or form;

they did not know that the nature inherently possesses all dharmas as conventional provisional phenomena. It is for this reason that our school refutes them in the following passage; it is not that our school [rejects the existence of phenomena].

They merely discuss the inherent presence of all phenomena (*dharmas*) as conventional designations, yet fail to clarify the essence of nature (*svabhāva*). Since the essence and magnitude of nature have vanished into extinction and quiescence, recent scholars have been unable to fathom its cause;

they speak only of the inherent presence of phenomena, describing their characteristics as distinct and vivid, thereby slandering the essence of nature as being devoid of characteristics and extinguished.

Thus, what is taught in the various texts of this school regarding the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the extinction [of characteristics]— *Note: The final phrase "實相空中亡" (the true reality, emptiness, and extinction) appears to be an incomplete or elliptical conclusion to the preceding critique.*

If [the principle] were obliterated and unobtainable, it would then become a mere empty fiction. ○ Now, following the phrase "on the contrary," the next section clarifies the present meaning; the text is divided into three parts.
First is the general establishment:
"On the contrary, this meaning lacks a name in the conventional sense; names are established in accordance with the Truth."

"Contrary" means to oppose and not to accord with. The ancient masters were biasedly attached to the fact that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is nameless while the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) possesses names;
they did not realize that although the ultimate truth is fundamentally nameless, it nonetheless encompasses all names.

Therefore, the present [text] opposes and does not accord with the ancient masters, clarifying instead that the conventional world is fundamentally nameless and that all names are established in accordance with the ultimate truth’s inherent presence of all names.
These are merely names. Next, the section beginning with "What is it that... provides a specific demonstration. What is it?
For example, at the beginning of the kalpa, when all things were vast and empty and there were no characters, the Sage looked up to the True Dharma and established conventional designations below.
According to principle, he was able to penetrate [reality]: by relying on the Truth, he named the Way; by relying on the Truth, he named Treasures as being noble and precious.

Principle (*li*) is able to encompass all; because it relies on the True (*zhen*), it is called a "net" (*wang*). Just as principle is able to give rise to responses, because it relies on the True, it is called an "echo" (*xiang*).
Regarding the phrase "the beginning of the kalpa," this refers to the start of the *vivartakalpa* (the aeon of formation). "Vast" (*kuo*) means empty (*kong*) or void (*xu*).

Now, that which is empty and void is precisely the beginning of the *vivartakalpa*, when all things have no names and are thus termed "empty and vast. Therefore, the subsequent line says "ten thousand... [referring to the myriad things].
"Things have no names" does not mean that during the kalpa of emptiness (*śūnyakalpa*) all was utterly void; rather, it is because within the kalpa of emptiness there were no things.
Now, we discuss the beginning of the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*): although things exist, they lack names by which they may be summoned; therefore, it is said to be "utterly void.

Because the Sage follows the supreme track of the True Dharma which is inherently complete, he says: "Looking upward, one accords with the fundamental reality; looking downward, one conforms to worldly sentiments through names."

Because it summons phenomena, it is said that "looking downward" (俯立) refers to the following passage from "according with principle" (如理) onward, which sequentially demonstrates the matters of "looking upward" (仰則)—the true Dharma—and "looking downward"—conventional designations.
All instances of saying "according with principle" refer to the fact that the true Dharma is inherently complete when one looks upward.
All instances of saying "named based on the true" refer to conventional designations established when looking downward. Looking upward, the truth is the fundamental reality.
Possessing the name "ability to penetrate" (nengtong) as a conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it relies on what is fundamentally present in reality (*tathatā*) and accords with worldly sentiment;
thus, by means of the name "ability to penetrate," it establishes itself as the Way (*mārga*), for that which is able to penetrate is itself the path.

Looking upward, it possesses the name "nobility" (*guizui*) as a conventional truth, relying on what is fundamentally present in reality and accords with worldly sentiment; thus, by means of the name "nobility," it establishes itself [as the Way].

Regarding "precious and noble," it is because they are truly jewels; looking upward, they rely on the name "comprehensive" (gai-lo) which signifies that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is inherently complete and the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is encompassed therein;
looking downward, they conform to worldly sentiment by establishing the term "net" (jāla) based on that name of "comprehensiveness.
Since "comprehensiveness" (gai-lo) is synonymous with a "net" (jāla), looking upward, the ultimate truth is inherently complete while the conventional truth arises as its responsive manifestation.
The name relies upon what is truly and inherently possessed, yet it accords with worldly convention to give rise to a responsive designation and establish a sound.

This "giving rise to a response" is precisely like an echoing answer. Although the text enumerates four matters in succession, it is specifically by means of the second—the preciousness of conforming to principle and relying on the true—which is termed a "jewel," that it clarifies how the three characters of this sutra’s specific title establish a name by referring to these actual things.
This is because the Sage, looking upward, follows the true principle that the essence of reality inherently possesses phenomenal functions, thus employing the noble name "Jinbao" (Golden Treasure);
yet, looking downward, he accords with worldly sentiment by establishing a distinct title using the conventional designation "Jinguangming" (Golden Light).
Therefore, the preceding text states: "Because there is a cause and condition, it may also be spoken of by taking 'Gold' as its name. Thus, it is named.

Indeed, it stands above all other treasures; if this is so, is it not because names exist within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)? Thus, the *Xuánqiān* states: "Since this treatise now discusses the conventional truth, one must distinguish names;
yet one need only understand that these conventional names are fundamentally possessed by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
How could one not believe that what is possessed is provisional? This refers to the three characters of the specific title of the present sutra.
The names of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) arise entirely from the fact that the essence of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is inherently present;

they are established by conforming to worldly sentiments based upon this inherent presence in the ultimate. Is it not just so when using dharmas as metaphors? In the seventh fascicle of the *Miaoxuan*, the Lotus is explained as follows:

"The lotus is not a metaphor" (meaning it is not a metaphor used to approximate a dharma); it receives its name from its own essential nature, similar to the myriad things at the beginning of a kalpa.
The nameless sages observed the principles and standards to establish names, just as a spider draws out silk to weave its web;
they modeled their actions after these patterns, like the wind driving a floating plant, or relying on them to fashion a chariot.

They launched rafts upon the currents to build boats, and traced the tracks of birds to form written characters—all were matters regulated by following the underlying principles. Please examine these words concerning how principles regulate affairs.
One should know that the three characters of this sutra’s specific title are the names for the functions established by the principle inherently present in phenomena.
How can it be said that they merely attach to the text? They are indeed names that attach to phenomena, yet when taken as the essence itself, they are names that summon the underlying principle.
Siming stated: "That which has a name in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) refers to the two truths of beginning and end in the Perfect Teaching."

Because it is inconceivable (*acintya*), it is called only the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*); because the Ultimate Truth is endowed with all virtues, it is said that the Ultimate Truth has a name.
As for the "Conventional Truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*) being "nameless," this refers to the Two Truths possessed by those of the three preceding teachings and all ordinary beings;
because these are conceivable (*cintya*), they are called merely "conventional. Since this conventionality is false and lacks real names or meanings, it is called "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*).
It is said that the *satya* (truth) is nameless; however, we now maintain that this is not so. Why? Regarding what is called the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), it is fundamentally nameless.

As for establishing names in accordance with the ultimate (*paramārtha*), this is because the conventional truth itself originally lacks names, yet by following the ultimate truth—which inherently possesses all names—one establishes conventional designations.
This is precisely the dual truth of emotion and wisdom (*jñāna*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*). Why? Because it follows wisdom, the essence of the ultimate truth...

Originally nameless, yet possessing names for the functional utility of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one accordingly establishes the names of the various dharmas of conventional truth in accordance with sentient beings' dispositions.

Since this is a correct elucidation of the conventional as being identical to the ultimate (*paramārtha*), how could one take the ordinary persons of the three preceding teachings and contrast them with the Perfect Teaching to explain the two truths of emotion and wisdom (*sattva-jñāna*) as they appear in this text?
Looking upward, one conforms to the ultimate Dharma; looking downward, one establishes [the conventional].

The worldly designation "False Admiration" (Xiáng-yǎng) establishes the noble title of the True Dharma; how could this three-character appellation possibly refer to the ordinary persons of the three preceding teachings?
The preceding passage explained the analogy for the Dharma in a manner that was still somewhat indirect, concise, and partial toward the Hinayana;
yet in the present text, the Dharma itself is used as the analogy. Since the principle of the Dharma governs all phenomena, why would it suddenly pertain only to the three preceding teachings?
Question: Since the Four Ming masters stated that the True Truth (*satyadharmatā*) possesses all virtues, why do you now reject this? Answer:

Although the Four Ming masters spoke of the True Truth and its possession of virtues, they did not realize that "possessing virtues" is precisely the wondrous provisional (*prajñapti*). Because their view contradicts the various texts of our own school, we do not adopt it here.
Regarding the Four Ming masters' interpretation of "the principle that can penetrate" (*ruli nengtong*), they rely upon the True Truth...

Regarding the statement that "the Way is called 'shallow'": when the sages perceive that all phenomena possess a shallow and proximate aspect, they establish the conventional designation of "shallow" for the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) based on the profound and distant meaning of the true Dharma.
Just as a worldly road that can only pass through a small portion is termed a "shallow and proximate path" in the world compared to the path of ultimate reality, so it is here. Now, I ask:
If that is so, then names already exist within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); how could it be that conventional truth is originally without names?
Section III of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (the third part of the citations) is divided into four parts; first, the citation from the *Avataṃsaka*.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "Plowing fields, turning the plow, making clothes, and digging wells—all these were performed by sages.

Regarding the plow (*lèi*, pronounced *luì* [Lù duì qiè]) and the plowshare (*sì*, sound *sì*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "A *lèi* is a curved wooden tool for hand-plowing. The *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) states:
"All activities, both mundane and supramundane, are performed by Bodhisattvas. (Wenju)

The *Jì* (Record/Commentary) states: "As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says, when a world is first formed, whatever necessities for the livelihood of sentient beings are required, the Bodhisattva at that time acts as a craftsman;
he never constructs instruments for killing. Furthermore, the *Shìqiān* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhìyǐ*) states:

"Hòu Dí fashioned the boat (he was a minister of the Yellow Emperor); Wéi Fù fashioned the mortar and pestle (he was a minister of the Yellow Emperor); Chīyóu fashioned weapons (he was a minister of the Fire Emperor)."
The Yellow Emperor created the ceremonial crown; Rong Cheng (a minister of the Yellow Emperor) created the calendar; Qi Bo (a minister of the Yellow Emperor) created medicine;

Li Shou (a minister of the Yellow Emperor) created mathematics; Gao Yao (a minister of Yu Shun) created the penal system; Ji Zhong created the chariot; Bo Yi created the well; Meng Tian created the brush; Cai Lun created paper.
All that was created by the ancients was established according to the principles of the Way. ○ Next.
Citing the text of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* in two parts: first, the direct citation.

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "In the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are only names but no real meaning; in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are both names and real meanings."
Regarding the statement that "conventional truth has names but no reality," etc.: conventionally, there are originally no names.

Although conventional designations are established in accordance with the ultimate truth, these conventional names are merely provisional arrangements; the meaning underlying these names is ultimately not final.

Why is this? Because while the principle of suchness can penetrate all things, and the name "Path" is based upon that truth, how could this path universally penetrate everything within the mundane world?
The Way also has obstructions and is ultimately subject to decay and ruin; therefore, in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are only empty names without real meaning.
If the true absence of marks (*animitta*) inherently possesses the name "Way," then this name and its meaning are in fact universally pervasive and unimpeded throughout all things;
thus it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which possesses both name and real meaning. This is because [the Way] is inherent in nature (*prakṛti-prakḷpta*).

While the true name refers to the true meaning, it negates the conventional designations of the world which lack reality; since this is the case for the Way (Mārga), the other [terms] may be understood by analogy.
Following this, the text next employs reductio ad absurdum to refute [the opponent].
Inferring from this, what further confusion could there be regarding the fact that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) possesses names?

By inferring from the explicit text of this great sutra, what further confusion could there be concerning the fact that the ultimate truth is fundamentally endowed with both names and meanings—such that one might not believe it?
[The opponent] asks: "The great sutra merely states that the ultimate truth has names; how can you take 'existence' (or 'having') [to mean that it exists as a substantial entity]?"

Regarding the statement that "the instruments [of existence] are explained as false," the instruments themselves are provisional (*prajñapti*), and the provisional is itself existence. Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Avalokana-sūtra-śāstra*:
"If there are already inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*), are there also inherent evils? The answer is that they are both fully present.
Furthermore, since all the texts of our school point to the inherent nature as being "existence," we know that in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the True Truth (*tattva*) possesses names.
"Existence" (*yu*) means "endowment" (*ju*). ○ Third, citing the text of Nāgārjuna also consists of two parts: first, the actual citation.
Nāgārjuna, the Bodhisattva of the Four Reliances, established names according to their underlying meaning and principle.
The *Zhiguan* quotes the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), stating: "A Bodhisattva relies on and follows the scriptural teachings to establish names;
this is called the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). There is no fault in establishing such names. In the current text, the character "yún" (says) is missing beneath the name "Nāgārjuna.
Since the *Śāstra* was composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, we know that in the current text, the person and the teaching are being cited alternately.
Regarding the one called Nāgārjuna: at the time of his birth, he was beneath a tree; because he attained the Way through a dragon (*nāga*), he is called Nāgārjuna.
"Dragon" refers to the *dharmakāya*, and "tree" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*.

He is also called Nāgabodhi, or alternatively, "dragon" is the Chinese term and "tree" is the Sanskrit term, translated as "Fierce" (*Ming*). He appeared three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and lived for seventy [years].

Regarding the "one hundred years" (and so forth), as for the four reliances (*catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāni*), there are two explanations. The first [explanation] is: that which precedes the stages of abiding (*vihāra*) is called the first reliance;

from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the fifth stage is called the second reliance; the sixth and seventh stages are called the third reliance; and from the eighth stage up to the tenth stage is called the fourth reliance.

The second [explanation] is: that which precedes the stages of abiding is called the first reliance; the ten stages are called the second reliance; and the [eleventh] stage is called the third reliance.

The practice of the ten stages of dedication (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*) is called the third reliance (*tṛtīya-pratisaraṇa*), and equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is called the fourth reliance (*caturtha-pratisaraṇa*).
These four reliances are both the stage of the teacher and the stage of the disciple (and so forth). Regarding the meaning, the following section explains the intent.
"Meaning" (*yi*) refers to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), and "principle" (*li*) refers to the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).

To say that names are established in accordance with meaning and principle means that they are established in accordance with the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)—the true principle of *tathatā* whose essence is fundamentally without marks (*animitta*) yet possesses conventional designations; thus, various titles are established in accordance with worldly convention. Therefore, it is said: [text continues].

"Meaning" (*yi*) refers to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), and "principle" (*li*) refers to suchness (*tathatā*). Question: How is it known that Nāgārjuna spoke of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) as being fundamentally devoid of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*)?
Answer: The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) cites the *Śāstra* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), which states: "The Buddha-dharma has two truths:
the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) possesses marks, while the ultimate truth is markless. How much more so does Nāgārjuna speak of the ultimate truth?

Since the sutras and treatises of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are thus regarding the signlessness (*animitta*) of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), we know that only when ultimate truth is fundamentally devoid of all signs can it fully possess the names and marks of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
That this "possession" is precisely what constitutes the provisional (*prajñapti*)—is this not so?

Therefore, one must not see the presence of dharmas within ultimate truth and immediately conclude that the characteristics of the principle-body (*tattva-śarīra*) are manifestly distinct. As the *Wenju ji* states: "The present school..."
Based on the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, according to the principle and the meaning, one contemplates the nature of mind to establish these two kinds of emptiness; this should be understood.

That passage, according to its principle and meaning, is what the present text calls "meaning," which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and "principle," which is the suchness of reality (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, according to the principle, contemplating the nature of mind is the contemplation of true suchness (*tathatā*); when contemplating the principle, one penetrates only the dharma-nature and nothing more.

The remaining applications follow this principle: when the mind takes the nature of the mind as its object, it is simply *vijñapti-mātra*. As one examines each phenomenon through the four natures (*catasraḥ svabhāvāḥ*), not even one can be found;

therefore, it is so called. Thus, regarding the true path, one must be proficient in the cultivation of the nature. This nature is inherently empty of both [self and phenomena], which is precisely the virtue of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*).

Therefore, the "object of the virtue of nature" at the beginning of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* refers to the contemplation of principle (*li-kan*); it is solely the penetration of the *dharmatā*, for the *dharmatā* functions spontaneously.
Possessing the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), one does not need to wait for the sequential examination of phenomena one by one to realize them;
yet, if one enters emptiness through such sequential examination, this is the realm of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) within the Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) system.

Because one only reaches the two kinds of emptiness after sequentially examining the four natures (*catvāraḥ svabhāvāḥ*), it should be known that, according to the principle, this is the contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā-vipaśyanā*), and according to the meaning, it is the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra-vipaśyanā*). Thus, the *Fuxing* [Commentary] states:
The present text follows the sutra and expands upon its meaning to provide detailed contemplative methods (*vipaśyanā*).

Thus, each of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is analyzed through four natures to render them like space. The reason for doing so is that, by analyzing them according to their meaning, one realizes that the dharmas such as the four great elements possess none of the natures of self, other, and so forth.
Therefore, it should be known that if one attains this principle, as stated in the "Exemplification of Meaning" (*yili*), one penetrates solely through the ultimate truth (*li*).

When the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is no longer engaged through other modes, but one focuses exclusively on the four ungraspable natures of the arising mind, then this constitutes the cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) section.
The ten vehicles of wondrous contemplation do not transcend what is subsumed within the two contemplations of *tathatā* (suchness) and *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Why is this?
For in various texts, if it says "to contemplate phenomena alone is the nature of phenomena, the dharma-realm, the true mark, or suchness," this refers to contemplating principle.
Furthermore, it is as if one were to say that through the investigation of the four phases and the four natures, one realizes the two kinds of emptiness;

this wondrous principle of the dharma-nature is precisely the "examination of phenomena through the perspective of consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). Both the contemplation of phenomena and the contemplation of principle are fully explained in the *Yuan-tong ji* (Record of Perfect Penetration) on the *Ten Non-dual Gates*. (And so forth.)
Fourth, citing the text of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* is also divided into two parts: first, the actual citation.
The *Vimalakīrti* states: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
Both ignorance (*avidyā*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) are termed "non-abiding," and both the conditions of defilement and purity are termed "establishing dharmas. Since this present text...
It clarifies that the Sage, through his wisdom, internally realizes the True Truth while externally accords with the conditions of sentient beings, provisionally establishing conventional names;
one should know that the Dharma-nature must be taken as the fundamental purity, upon which all established dharmas depend. (The section on) Sūtras and Śāstras concludes below by exhorting faith.
The sutras and śāstras are unanimous on this point; how could one not believe it?
By "sutras" is meant the great *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and by "śāstras" is meant Nāgārjuna’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*. "Unanimous" means that they are all thus:
within these sutras and śāstras, it is all discussed that the conventional has no name inherently, and names are established only in accordance with the ultimate truth.
Now that you have studied the Buddha’s teachings, how could you possibly fail to believe the sincere words of the sūtras and śāstras of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
Second, the following section provides a formal commentary on the text, which is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies that the title of the sūtra is an analogy for "the Dharma as it is."
Now, that which is called the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is worthy of honor and esteem; thus the nature of phenomena is named "Gold.

This nature of phenomena is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, and is thus named "Light. This nature of phenomena possesses great compassion and is able to bring manifold benefit, and is thus named "Radiance.
This is precisely the Dharma-gate of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
The previous statement that "the noble is according to principle" corresponds to the present text’s statement that "the dharma of *dharmatā* is worthy of honor and esteem.
The previous statement that "it is called a treasure by relying on the truth" corresponds to the present text’s statement that "*dharmatā*" is named "gold.
Since it is thus that gold is established by relying on the truth, one should know by analogy that the name "light" is established based on its own essence; it is the actual reality itself.
When one uses the principle of provisional dharma to regulate matters, one takes the dharma itself as the analogy:

since the nature of gold is made into "Golden Light," how can it be said that the three-character title refers to a single dharma? If you say it is a single dharma, I do not know what you are pointing to as the analogy.
That which is called the "Dharma-gate of Golden Light" is a name established based on its own essence; it is not [a mere metaphor].
Obtaining gold from others is the name for that which is inherently present within the *dharmatā*;
because this serves as a gateway through which one can access the Great Way, we know that the three characters of the distinct title are precisely the dharma-gate of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
Therefore, the passage cited below—which states that "within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, I, Śākyamuni, am seen"—is intended to convey this very meaning.
Therefore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The designation 'Lotus' is not a metaphorical analogy (it is not a provisional borrowing used to illustrate a dharma);
rather, it is the subtle and wondrous name for the pure cause and effect of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-dharmaparyāya*.
To designate this dharmaparyāya as 'Lotus' is the name of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* itself. The present case is likewise so: the *dharmatā* is inherently endowed with nobility.

Because the Great Compassion of Quiescent Illumination benefits all beings, the three characters of the distinct title are established as the "Gate of Universal Access" (*nengtongmen*) to enable the realization that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently noble, quiescent, and illuminating; thus it is called a "Dharma-gate.
As for what is termed "Dharma," this Dharma refers to the teaching (*śāsana*), for although there is ultimately no speaking, that which is spoken necessarily constitutes a teaching.
This refers generally to the fact that whatever is spoken is termed "teaching" (*śāsana*).

If one were to discuss what is spoken in greater detail, the entire *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) being made into the precious and noble Golden Honored One is merely a metaphorical representation of taking the Dharma itself as the illustration.

Next, following the passage "The Bodhisattva enters this," the text clarifies how the various sages receive their names based on the *dharmamukha* (Dharma-gate) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. This section consists of two parts.
First, the actual clarification:
when a bodhisattva enters this dharma-gate, it is named after the dharma itself;

that is, the Bodhisattva *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light), the Buddha *Suvarṇottama* (Ultimate Golden Light), the Tathāgata *Suvarṇajvālāprabha* (Golden Flame Radiance), the Tathāgata *Suvarṇaśataprabhābhāsagarbha* (Treasury Illumined by a Hundred Golden Lights), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "entering this dharma-gate" and so forth: entering this refers to entering the three characters of *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (*Jin guangming*).
This is a name that is provisional yet identical to the real, a metaphorical representation of the Dharma, and a gate that enables penetration.

Because it is named according to that which is provisional yet identical to the real, and which serves as a metaphorical representation of the Dharma, it is called the Bodhisattva *Suvarṇaprabha*. It is also like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The Bodhisattva Zhonghuade (Chinese Virtue) also derives his name from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*; it is by taking the dharma itself as a metaphor that he receives his name according to its essential nature.
Because bodhisattvas attain [the fruit] partially while Buddhas attain it ultimately, there are such [Buddhas] as Suvarṇajvālāprabha Tathāgata.
Some people see the current passage stating that he "receives his name from the dharma" and fail to look at the subsequent text which states "taking the dharma itself as a metaphor."

One might then claim that the separate title refers merely to a single dharma, yet one fails to reflect upon this: if it were a single dharma, why would it be used as a metaphor? Furthermore, one fails to reflect upon this:
if it were a single dharma, it would be the basis [of the teaching]; why then would it be identified with the essence itself? Moreover, one fails to reflect upon this:
if it were a single dharma, how could it serve as a metaphor to illustrate the dharma for those of dull faculties? And furthermore—
If one does not contemplate this as a single dharma, it would be identical to the two characters "wondrous dharma" (*miaofa*) from the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Yet, how could that "wondrous dharma" ever have been spoken of in terms of its own essential substance? It is only upon reaching the interpretation of the lotus flower that one discusses its two meanings.

If the lotus flower is used as a metaphor for the wondrous dharma, is this not the present text using an analogy to correspond with the dharma? As for the formulation based on the principle of the dharma:

Regarding this matter, is it not the case that the current text uses the Dharma itself as a metaphor? Since the interpretation of the lotus flower already possesses both meanings [of cause and effect], this explanation of the gold and jewels is likewise so.

If one were to claim that the three characters in the specific title of this sutra constitute a "single dharma" (a single principle), how would one distinguish this from the *Miaoxuan*’s explanation of the "Wondrous Dharma"?
Therefore, we know that the current text proceeds from the perspective of the Dharma.
A name is merely a designation established by using the very phenomenon itself as a metaphor. ○ Regarding the passage "If this is so...
and below, the subsequent section explaining the doubt is divided into two parts; first, the doubt:
"If this is so, for what reason is he named Śākyamuni?"
If it is argued that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are named after the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (Golden Light) Dharma-gate, why is Śākyamuni not named "Golden Light" but instead named "Śākya"?
Regarding this, there are two parts to the subsequent explanation of the doubt: first, the direct explanation. "Śākya" has both general and specific meanings.
[The following is] the text explaining the doubt, which is divided into two sections; first, the direct explanation.
Śākyamuni has both general and specific names. From the perspective of the general name, he is called *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (Golden Light), which is identical to that of all Buddhas;
from the perspective of the specific name, he receives the title Śākyamuni.
One should know that this name "Śākyamuni" is derived from the specific, yet the specific necessarily possesses the general; therefore, it is said that Śākyamuni has this general [name].
The specific name is derived from the general; thus it is called *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light), which perfectly accords with the treasury of the Buddha’s hundredfold illuminating radiance.
While the general name is established through the specific, there is no contradiction in accepting the title *Śākyamuni* (the Sage of the Śākya clan).

If this is so, since the specific identity of Śākyamuni is already contained within the general category of all Buddhas, how could the general nature of all Buddhas not also contain the specific? Therefore, following the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha," the next [passage] is cited:
"Realization" refers to realizing that the specific epithet of Śākyamuni possesses the universal name, which is identical to that of all Buddhas.
This section is divided into three parts; first, citing the "Praise of the Buddha" chapter to demonstrate that the specific name possesses the universal.
Therefore, the "Chapter Praising the Buddha" states: "The body of the Tathāgata is golden and subtle; its brilliance shines forth. This "brilliance" is precisely light;
this praises the essence of the Buddha-dharma and does not praise worldly gold. It takes the nature of the Buddha-dharma as gold;
it does not borrow from worldly gold.
In the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha," since the various bodhisattvas and others praise the distinct name of Śākyamuni’s body as being golden,
subtle, and wondrous, with its brilliance shining forth, we know that although the distinct name is Śākyamuni, it does not preclude the general name *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (Golden Light).

If this were not the case, then the description of Śākyamuni’s body as being golden, subtle, and wondrous, with its brilliance shining forth— just like [the description of the Buddha in the title]— would be redundant.
How can this be reconciled? This is a praise of the essence of the Buddha-dharma; the body of the Buddha-dharma possesses the functional activity (*kāritra*) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
It is not a praise of worldly gold. Since the essential nature (*dharmatā*) is inherently endowed with the treasure of gold, it establishes its functional activity;
therefore, it does not praise worldly gold, for worldly gold possesses only the name of being "noble."
This is because there is no meaning of "reality" [in the conventional sense]. When it says "the Buddha-nature is gold," the character "dāng" (當) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).
This means that the essence of the Buddha’s self-realized *dharmatā* is inherently noble; thus, the Dharma itself is used as a metaphor and named "gold.
It does not borrow from worldly gold; it does not rely upon worldly gold to serve as a simile for the Dharma. Therefore, below...
The text states that "it is not a conventional [example]"; this is a metaphorical illustration (*upamā*) of the Buddha-dharma. This is precisely the intended meaning.

If one understands that the example is itself the Dharma, then establishing it in accordance with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), what is there that is improper about the gold of the mundane world?

However, because the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that while conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) has names, it lacks substantial reality, we provisionally set it aside. It conforms to the doctrine of inherent nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), which is why it is said to be "not [conventional]."

Praise to the World-Honored One of Golden Ears: To speak exhaustively, his nature is fundamentally nameless yet possesses all names; it is unspeakable, yet once spoken, it necessarily constitutes the teaching.
This Honored One of Noble Principle relies upon the True Reality as his foundation, yet he condescends to conform to the world by designating him with the name "Golden Treasure.
Thus, one should know that these general and specific names of the Buddha are all subsumed within the two truths of conventional sentiment and ultimate wisdom.

Because the ear is provisionally established in accordance with the world, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The principle of the dharma-nature (dharmatā) is neither ancient nor modern, neither fundamental nor derivative, neither real nor provisional;
it is only in relation to the dharma-nature that one discusses the fundamental and the derivative, the provisional and the real, the coarse and the subtle.
Thus, we know that it is only by means of conventional linguistic designations that there are past, future, and present; it does not mean that bodhi has coming and going.
Now, even the names "Dharmakāya" and "principle-nature" are still provisional designations established in accordance with worldly convention;
how could they not be conventional truths when the very essence of principle possesses them as metaphors for phenomena? Next, he cites the *Tri-kāya-parivarta* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as proof.
The *Chapter on the Three Bodies* states: "One is of the same substance as all Buddhas, of the same intention as all Buddhas, and of the same activity as all Buddhas.
Being of the same substance means sharing the same Dharma-nature gold; being of the same intention means sharing the same Dharma-nature light;
and being of the same activity means sharing the same Dharma-nature radiance. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All Tathāgatas are identical in their single Dharma-body; they are one body."
The single power of wisdom and the fearlessnesses are likewise: the body is identical to gold, wisdom is identical to light, and the powers and fearlessnesses are identical to brilliance.
Within the single essence of the Dharma, these three meanings are fully present; it is not that worldly gold is used as a mere metaphor to represent the Buddha-dharma.
"Distinctly, it must necessarily possess the universal and identical principle of the *dharmatā* of all Buddhas.

Because the Buddhas are all identical in possessing the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, it is called 'identical essence' (*samāna-kāya*). This 'identical essence' is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* which is the *dharmatā*.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is cited to establish this identical essence as possessing the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. Next, the passage beginning with 'From one body, that is... is the explanation of the *Avataṃsaka*."
The intent of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is to clarify that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* [Sūtra] refers to the *suvarṇa* (gold) of the single essence.

Regarding the fact that the three meanings are fully present within the single dharma-essence: although the dharma-essence is one, what prevents it from possessing the three meanings of "gold" and so forth?

It is precisely because raising one [meaning] immediately implies the three that this is not a case of borrowing the worldly metal "gold" as a metaphorical illustration for the nature and essence of the Buddha-dharma.
Third, the tree deity is cited to corroborate the specific title.
Thus, the tree deity says: "The immeasurable great compassion proclaims such a wondrous jewel-like sutra; its very substance is entirely this wondrous jewel.
This jewel is fully endowed with radiance; it is not by borrowing worldly gold that the Dharma is illustrated."
This is the Dharma-action. The *Pǐshùshén zàn* (Praise by the Tree Deity) says:

"Śākyamuni, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, has proclaimed such a wondrous and precious sūtra. It is called a "wondrous treasure" (*miaobao*) because gold is the most excellent among all treasures;
thus it is termed a "wondrous treasure. That this wondrous treasure is replete with radiance refers to the three characters of the specific title.

The two characters "sūtra" (經典) constitute the general title; thus, the four characters "wondrous jewel sūtra" (妙寶經典) represent both the specific and general titles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.

Since the conventional truth of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* teaching is established based on the fact that it is inherently present within the very substance of the dharma-nature, we know that this is merely using the dharma itself as a metaphor, rather than [using something else] to illustrate it.
Because it is used as an analogy for the Dharma, it is said that both the substance and its essence are wondrous jewels. These jewels are fully endowed with radiance;
they are not ordinary gold borrowed to serve as an analogy for the Dharma. Next, the analysis of the text is divided into two parts: first, the question.
Question: It has been said of old that this sutra is named after its parable; why do you now deviate from that and rely instead on the literal text?

My intention is as follows: since the preceding text already established that "I shall now explain the names as five," yet the third section refers to it as a "Parable" (Upamā), and the current text then points out that "it has been said of old that this sutra is named after its parable"—this [statement] has two meanings. First...
This [method] has been used by both ancient and modern scholars as an analogy for the Dharma; however, because the ancients' analogies were not exhaustive, the present school refutes them.
This does not mean that the ancients were incapable of using analogies to represent the Dharma.

Therefore, the present school points out the old [view], stating that while this sutra derives its name from an analogy, it does not hinder the present school’s own fivefold classification of the explanation of names. The third [section] therein is as follows:
Regarding this analogy: although both the ancients and the moderns employ analogies in the same way, the ancients’ use of analogies to represent the Dharma was already incomplete;

how then could they have been able to explain it? Because [the ancients] attached the analogy to the literal text rather than making the analogy correspond to the essence of the Dharma itself, we now refer to the old tradition, stating that this sutra derives its name from its analogy, and thus pose this question in contrast to our own school’s method of attaching the analogy to the text. Therefore:
What is meant by this? It refers to the charge of being hypocritical and deviant while relying on the literal text.

This does not mean that our school alone restricts itself to two interpretations—relying on the text and adhering to the essential substance—and discards the third interpretation, which uses analogies to illustrate the Dharma. What is the meaning of "hypocritical" (*jiao*) and "deviant" (*yi*)?

"Hypocritical" means deceitful; "deviant" means different. Why is it considered different from the ancients to merely employ the method of analogy while establishing names based solely on the literal text?
The "explanation based on the essential nature" (*dang-ti*) merely clarifies the name that attaches to the text and points to a specific phenomenon:
gold is the fundamental, inherent essence of the principle of *dharmatā*, which is merely gold established by provisional designation in accordance with worldly convention.

Therefore, by posing a question specifically regarding the attachment to the text, the explanation of the essential nature is naturally subsumed. Consequently, the response below still distinguishes two meanings, the first of which concerns the attachment to the text.

Regarding the response through analogy, following the sequence of the answer, one should further understand that while the question refers to the traditional view that this sutra is named after its analogies—
posing the inquiry from the perspective of the present school’s attachment to the literal text—
the subsequent answer addresses both the present school’s use of analogies to represent the Dharma and the attachment to the literal text as the actual essence.

Answer: Therefore, the subsequent text states that the meaning is inferred as being remote; it quotes the *Śūnyatā-parivarta*, saying, "For the sake of those with dull faculties, he gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
This is precisely that intended meaning. Thus, it further clarifies that using analogies to represent the Dharma has been practiced by both ancient and modern masters alike;
it is simply that the ancients' analogies for the Dharma were not exhaustive, and thus they were refuted by the present school. Next, the answer to the text is divided into two parts.
The initial section, which correlates the text with metaphors to provide an analogical response, is further divided into two parts. First is the direct response:
it is not that the present text contradicts the metaphor, nor is it that adhering dogmatically to the metaphor contradicts the text;
rather, there are two paths, and both must be preserved.
It is not that our school establishes an "exegesis based on the text" (*fùwén shì*) by following the scriptural words and thereby harms the principle of using metaphors to illustrate the Dharma.
If one were to recklessly and exclusively cling to using metaphors to illustrate the Dharma, one would likewise harm the principle of basing names upon the specific facts indicated in the text.
Examining the reasons for this, there are two paths; a "path" (*tú*) is a way (*dào*). It is thus.

Therefore, one should know that both the use of analogies to illustrate the Dharma and the adherence to the literal text must be preserved together; it is not permissible to restrict oneself to a single-sided dogmatic attachment.

As stated previously by the Fourth Master (Siming), the Great Master followed ancient precedents and employed others' use of analogies, yet since the titles of the sutras are not analogies but the Dharma itself, he later established his own two-fold interpretation in the subsequent text:
"adherence to the text" (*fu-wen*) and "the actual substance" (*dang-ti*), which remains valid to this day.
In the text, it is further explained: "The current interpretation of the scripture’s title preserves two meanings; therefore, neither of these two approaches should be discarded.
You, by adhering exclusively to the metaphorical, abandon the intimate for the remote; I, by preserving both, ensure that both the intimate and the remote are attained.
Now, I say this explanation is contradictory and difficult to understand. Why? Because previously it was said that one follows the ancients and accords with the usage of others.
For example, since the title of the sutra is a dharma and not a metaphor, why do you now ask, "Why do you say that the current explanation of the sutra title exists with two meanings?
Furthermore, since it is said that the sutra title is not a metaphor but a dharma, this would necessarily be interpreted as a single dharma alone;
why then do you now say, "Neither of the two paths should be discarded"? Since you have already spoken of these two paths...

One must not neglect either side by arbitrarily declaring that this is the actual teaching and that the analogy is not. Since the text explicitly states it is not [the actual teaching], why would one now, based on the literal wording, undermine the analogy?
Why would one stubbornly cling to the literal text while abandoning the preceding analogy of the Dharma?
Later students, mired in ignorance, merely transmit what they have heard according to the sound of the words; upon hearing the teachings of Siming, they immediately claim he was a "Subordinate Sage."

It is truly lamentable that one cannot distinguish between what is good and what is not. Therefore, as previously stated, the subsequent passage cites the preceding text to demonstrate that there are two paths regarding the meaning of "intimacy" (*qīnshū*):
first, it was said that in terms of meaning, the distant is inferred; second, according to the text, the intimate is relied upon.
Although both [the literal and the metaphorical] coexist within the text, they are not devoid of the distinction between the near and the distant.

Therefore, the third [section] uses a metaphor to illustrate the meaning of the distant, while the fourth relies on the explicit text to clarify the near. Furthermore, it must be stated that although there is a distinction between the near and the distant, neither may be discarded;
if one were to discard either side, it would constitute a violation of the text by the metaphor, or an adherence to the metaphor that harms the text.
This is the "Exposition" (vyañjana); thus it is clear from the preceding text where it states, "Now, explaining the names, there are five," that this point is being elucidated here.

○ Regarding the section beginning with "If one has dull faculties," the text provides an answer by correlating the essence of each stage with a metaphor; this response consists of three parts, the first of which is the direct answer.
If those of dull faculties use analogies to illustrate the Dharma, while those of sharp faculties take the Dharma itself as the analogy:

when those of dull faculties use an analogy to illustrate the Dharma, it refers to the third section above, which uses the analogy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) for all horizontal and vertical Dharma-gates;
whereas when those of sharp faculties take the Dharma itself as the analogy, this refers to the fifth section of the preceding text.
The essence itself is the True Dharma (paramārtha-satya), which inherently possesses the names for the phenomenal functions of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
thus, it is metaphorically designated by the three characters of *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. This is because the three characters of the specific title are merely names for phenomenal functions.
For those of dull faculties, they take this metaphor to represent all phenomena, whether horizontal or vertical; however, those of sharp faculties realize that it is [the essence itself].
Because these three characters are used as a metaphor for the Dharma, the previous passage simply stated that "gold" serves as the name;

this does not contradict the current text’s intention regarding the sharp and dull faculties. Therefore, there is no impediment to the three characters of the distinct title serving both the sharp and dull roots for understanding.
For this reason, since the text consistently uses the word "if" (*ruo*), how could this not be the distinct title?

These three characters are merely included within the category of single metaphors; yet when people hear these three characters from the distinct title of this sutra, they immediately raise the objection:
"How is this different from the ancient masters? Alas, how lamentable! Their ignorance is profound indeed.
Even the ancient masters' use of metaphors to represent the Dharma was already incomplete; how could they have known to compose [the title] by taking the Dharma itself as the metaphor?
It is like the analogy of the Four Clarities (*caturvidha-vyakti*).

Those of sharp faculties know that this can serve as an analogy for the worldly *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light), because it is the sages who, by looking up to the True Dharma, established its name; thus, "sharp faculties" is an analogy for the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*).
Now, if this is so, since the True Dharma itself constitutes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, then sharp faculties themselves constitute the Dharma-practice analogy.

Is it not the case that the separate title is a single analogy? If one were to say that the separate title is a single dharma, then one would have to change it to "the dharma itself acting as the dharma.
Furthermore, if gold and other such things are definitively established as dharmas, how could they be used as analogies to correspond to the dharmas for those of dull faculties?
Now, it is certain that the three characters of the separate title are the analogies, [intended] for those of dull faculties.

Thus, by means of this analogy, the dharmas of horizontal and vertical [orientation] and so forth are illustrated; if one possesses sharp faculties, one will realize that these are the very dharmas themselves.
This passage follows the logic of the text, making the principle manifest and easy to perceive. Why do worldly people stubbornly cling to their views and remain lost in confusion?
The subsequent section introduces scriptural evidence.
The subsequent text states: "Abiding within the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one shall behold me, Śākyamuni, within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-parivarta*) says: "Out of compassion for those of dull faculties, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)."
Now that the title has been explained, the text points to the following passage of the scripture, namely, what is said in the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" (*Devatāparivarta*) below:
"Abiding within this profound *dharmatā*, one shall behold me, Śākyamuni, within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
This is a proof for those of sharp faculties; it is an analogy wherein the Dharma itself serves as the illustration of Śākyamuni.

Although the designation [of this analogy] is derived from a specific context, we must now take that specific instance as necessarily encompassing the general principle in order to clarify the explanation of the metaphor.
Thus, the preceding text, citing the *Praise of the Buddha* (*Buddhastotra*), states: "The body of the Tathāgata is golden and subtle; its radiance shines forth... [and so on].

"The person of dull capacity clings to the finger" provides three illustrations below.

The dull-witted person clings to the finger or guards the stump; how could they know of the hare or the moon? The sharp-witted person attains liberation through suspension and has no need for the stump or the finger (and so forth).
Regarding the finger pointing at the moon, as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "The teachings of the sūtras are like the finger pointing at the moon.

As for the stump and the hare, the *Fǔxíng* (Sub-commentary) cites an account from the Song dynasty: there was a farmer who, while plowing in a field, saw a hare strike a stump and die. Thereafter, he abandoned his farming and constantly waited for another hare to come.
He sat guarding this stump, hoping that another rabbit would again run into it. A bystander advised him against it, yet he refused to stop.
Thus, popular tradition refers to those who persist in delusion as "stump-guarders. Since the case of the stump-guarder is thus, the analogy of the finger is likewise so.

The finger is originally intended to point toward the moon; yet, instead of looking at the moon, one merely guards the finger. Therefore, by merely guarding the finger, one does not see the moon; this serves as the analogy.
The case of the man guarding the stump who failed to see the hare is likewise so; therefore, it is now rejected as an analogy for those of dull faculties who stubbornly cling to it.

To use this as a metaphor for the Dharma is like pointing at the stump instead of reaching for the hare; it cannot compare to the sharp faculties that can understand by taking the Dharma itself as the metaphor.

Thus it is said: "How could one know the hare and the moon? Here, "how" (ning) means "how could" (qi). Those of sharp faculties attain transcendental awakening by taking the Dharma itself as the metaphor.
For this reason, it is said that "liberation is suspended [in the air]," meaning there is no need for the trouble of using analogies to model the Dharma;
thus, it is called "not requiring [analogies]. The commentary states: "Those of sharp faculties achieve suspended liberation; they take the Dharma itself as the analogy.

Although there is no need to use an analogy to model the Dharma, one must not allow this to invalidate the case of those with dull faculties who rely on analogies to model the Dharma. Why? Because it is attached to the literal text.

Regarding the fact that both the dharma and its analogies must coexist as the actual substance, and that both the dharma and its analogies must likewise be established together—because I feared people would not understand the intent of this dual coexistence—I have thus provided the commentary. Therefore, the *Miaoxuan* states:

"Those of sharp faculties immediately understand the principle through names alone, without relying on analogies," which corresponds to what is said here: "Those of superior capacity attain immediate understanding."
There is no need for a literal or restrictive interpretation. What is called "sharp faculty" (li-gen) refers precisely to one who understands the principle;

this is merely a name applied to their engagement with phenomena, where they intuitively comprehend the principle while still within the realm of things. It is simply a metaphorical designation for the dharma. Thus, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The principle of the dharma governs phenomena.

Since the present text says that those of sharp faculties intuitively comprehend [the truth] without needing a restrictive interpretation, and the *Miaoxuan* likewise speaks of "sharp faculties," [the two sources are in agreement].
This is precisely what is meant by "understanding the principle without relying on metaphors"; thus one knows that this section of analysis cannot be said to have been arbitrarily added by another.

Question: In the *Miaoxuan*, it is clarified that those of superior faculties only require the metaphor of the lotus flower for their understanding, whereas those of middle and lower faculties who have not yet awakened must rely on the metaphor of the grass flower;
therefore, there are three cycles of teaching to accommodate the superior, middle, and lower faculties.

The current text merely distinguishes between those of sharp and dull faculties; how could there be a threefold distinction of superior, middling, and inferior? The pattern of the response must likewise be so. Why is this?
Within the text, both the new and old versions cite three passages that clarify the central theme:

when people of superior faculties hear the four Buddhas dispel their doubts, they realize that what was long distant is fundamentally difficult to exhaust; when people of middling faculties hear the Prince clarify [the matter]...
The legs of mosquitoes and gnats can serve as city towers; mice may climb a ladder made of rabbit horns; and the Asuras may devour the moon. Yet, the Dharma-body has no *śarīra*.
When those of inferior capacity hear Śākyamuni’s discourse on the three bodies, he explains them extensively through broad differentiation.
This is the clear textual evidence that the three cycles of teaching were designed to accommodate those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities. Next, the Contemplation of the Mind.

Regarding the "Explanation of Names" (*Shimíng*): this passage on the contemplation of the mind (*guānxīn*), along with the preceding analysis and the subsequent re-elucidation of the meaning of the sovereign (*dìwáng*), was previously claimed by the masters of Qiántáng to have been arbitrarily added by later generations rather than being the personal teaching of the Great Master.

However, Sìmíng defended it through several rounds of debate (as detailed in the *Yǔánmù*). Now, I maintain that as long as the contemplation of the mind is preserved, it is beneficial; it is not merely a matter of counting jewels in vain.

Therefore, while the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) and the *Fahua Wenju* (Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) both first explain according to the teachings (*jiao*) and subsequently clarify contemplative practice (*guanxing*), since the *Wenju* of the present sutra already exists as a commentary on the contemplation of the mind (*guansin*), how could its *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning) consist merely of explanations according to the teachings?孤山 (Gushan) said:
"I observe that its wording is prolix yet lacks essentials, and its substance is coarse with little elegance; those who devote their minds to literary composition will know this upon reading it."
If the words are not those of the former [author] and the calligraphy is not that of the former [author], then the true and the false can be distinguished;
how could one wait until having immersed oneself in Buddhist studies before being able to judge right from wrong? To say now that this is not so—why?
If it is claimed that this text is verbose and lacks essentials, this is merely to criticize the previous correct commentary for its analysis of the ten types of [spurious works].

If you claim that these three dharmas are broad yet flavorless, or that this text is substantial but lacks literary refinement, then one might as well criticize the various texts on contemplative practice, such as the *Śikṣānanda-śāstra* (Guanxin lun) and others;
compared to the present text, their language would appear even more austere.
Furthermore, the *Fahua wenju* states, "This is ultimate emptiness," so how could one possibly find fault with it?

Regarding the literary composition, following the standard of Siming, I have preserved the commentary on the contemplation (*guan*); however, there are some differences between this and the analysis of the meaning through topical divisions (*ke*).
Within this, there are two parts: first, the heading;
